utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Court Deputy, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we hear the next witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention to this Bench? I -- yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is -- sorry, did I interrupt Your Honour then? Were you about to say something else? I just jumped up to my feet. Your Honours, yes, look, there is a couple of matters to raise. Your Honours may have received at about 6.30 last night a list of -- of documents that the Prosecution would seek to use in evidence with this witness. Now, some of those are going to be contentious in the case, and I just thought it would be wise to raise those at an early stage, rather than embarrass the witness in the middle of his evidence in relation to these matters. Sometimes witnesses feel as if it's an attack on them when a document they produced is questioned. And that's not the case at all here. But what I thought was I should raise a couple of preliminary matters and see what is the best way to deal with them, whether -- whether to deal with some of these matters at the start or whether to deal with them in the running. Now, first of all, could I just inquire, does Your Honour have -- do Your Honours have in front of you the -- the outline of Prosecution exhibits to be tendered or to be used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid not, but I could find it from my computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, could I just -- perhaps I'll -- I can proceed while that's being found, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The documents are -- that the Prosecution wishes to use in cross-examination here include the following documents: A diary of Sefko Hodzic. Now, that's not in evidence as yet, but it's Prosecution 65 ter number 106. That's a diary. The next document that the Prosecutor wants to put into evidence that -- that's relevant to Hodzic himself are some articles that he wrote in a newspaper called Oslobodjenje, and he wrote those articles in 1999. So, Your Honour, could I just indicate, when you look at that list that you -- that you have in front of you, the ones I'm talking about are -- the first three documents are all orders, as you'll see, and those documents are all, I take it, documents that the witness has seen at some stage and so therefore he would comment about -- just as long as he's seen them, I'm not going to make any objection about it. Two of them are in evidence in any event already. The diary of Hodzic is the fourth document listed there. Ignore number 5 for the moment, because that's a different category. The sixth one, 65 ter number 126, are articles by Sefko Hodzic on the 20 -- that were written and published in 1999, in January and February of 1999. The next document is a audiotape produced by Sefko Hodzic on the 5th of the 10th, 2000, and that is said to be using the Sanction system. And finally, there are some excerpts to be taken from the Hodzic book, which was produced, and that's -- the English translation of that is the opened -- the unsealed envelope, and that's 65 ter number 183. Now, Your Honours, after those Hodzic documents, if you'd go back to MFI281, you'll see that it's going to be sought to tender a part of a book by Sefer Halilovic into evidence here through this witness. And I raise some preliminary objections to that being done yesterday in dealing with the -- I don't know if it was yesterday, but it was in dealing with the previous witness. Now, the issues I want to raise are as follows: Some of them are mere housekeeping; some of them are questions that go to the use of documents in court. The question of whether they are admitted into the evidence, I understand, are quite different, and I'm dealing now with issues as to whether they should be used in court at all at this stage. Could I mention first of all on the second page the transcript -- the audio transcript. Now, I take it with respect to that the evidence will be that this is actually a copy of an original that was made at the time. And if it is -- if that's the case and if Mr. Hodzic indicates that that's the case, then, of course, there's no admission to implying in court a contemporaneous document. But I note with some concern the reemergence of the Sanction method, and I just wonder how long is the passage that that's -- that's going to be used via Sanction. If it's just simply to be used playing contemporaneously and having the -- the transcript go along with it, then there's no difficulty with it so long as in -- in the fullness of time that document is in the -- in the e-court system. But as indicated, we've got an e-court system going here, and we were happy to allow the Prosecutors to -- to agree to the Prosecutors using Sanction in limited circumstances with short documents. So that perhaps the learned Prosecutor can -- can clarify what the situation is as regards that matter. Now, to proceed to the -- to the next ones. We have a concern about these newspaper articles, Your Honours, that are proposed to be shown to the witness. I've obviously been provided with these, and I've read them, and I know what's contained in them. And the newspaper articles and the book contain information that's broadly similar. But as to the newspaper articles, Your Honours, the Prosecutors are on record in this case in a filing dated the 30th of August of last year - and this was a Prosecutor's response to the Defence motion for access to personal files and other materials dated 30th of August - on page 2 of that, at footnote number 3, the learned Prosecutor at the time asserted a position that articles in a newspaper cannot be deemed to be credible evidence, and that was the Prosecution's position then, and we are concerned about it. Now, there are some cases where newspaper articles are relevant and helpful to the Court, but here these ones are written many years later; in this case, over six years later -- or sorry, over five years later, at the start of 1999. And I'm concerned about they being produced in evidence and used in evidence. And the reason I'm concerned about it is this, Your Honour: That what we think should happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's all right. I'm following you. This computer is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What -- what my concern is simply this: I just want to preserve the oral character of this trial and -- and the ability of -- of Mr. Halilovic to follow and -- and the ability of the Court, frankly, to assess the evidence a proper and orderly way. What we submit is that the witness should give his evidence of what he saw, and to the extent that it's relevant, what he did and who he met, and all of the other things he can say, many of which are highly relevant to this case, as to what happened. If he's having trouble remembering, then we don't have any objection to him refreshing his memory from contemporaneous documents, and, for example, the diary, which we presume is a contemporaneous document, would be perfectly appropriate for him to look at and say, "Well, I can't remember exactly what date it was. May I look at the diary?" Yes, of course. And the Defence would obviously be very happy for that to be done. To allow him to look at newspaper articles in that regard just seems to be a -- a controversial thing to do, bearing in mind that these newspaper articles are all much later. And it exposes me to a situation, frankly, in cross-examining that do I then need to cross-examine a witness in 2005 on something he did halfway between this period and to say, "Look, Witness, has your memory changed?" And he might say, "I was telling the truth the best I could." And then if he's pressed, he'll probably say, "I had a diary to look at," that was a contemporaneous diary. So in that situation, obviously the contemporaneous diary is the one that he should look had. The other reason I'm concerned, frankly, is that witnesses when shown something they've written in the past might completely, honestly, and without any desire to be untruthful adopt what they've said, and they obviously have a natural human proclivity not to want to retreat from that. I just don't want to be in the position of having to cross-examine somebody on something he wrote very much later, long after these I events were finished, and therefore I've got concerns about that newspaper articles. I don't have concern about his evidence on those topics, and I'm not saying that what he talked about there was irrelevant. That's not the objection. It is relevant, and the Prosecutor is entitled to lead the evidence concerning those events. So I just want to be clear that it's an objection about these articles rather than about other things. So that's what I've got the to say about those articles. They're not contemporaneous, and that in the first instance the witness should be given the chance to simply -- to give the evidence that he has about those topics and -- and then perhaps see where we go from there. That's what I have to raise about the newspaper articles. Now, I turn to the book. Again, it may be that the book has more relevance than the newspaper articles because it may be that the witness is -- has used -- has -- has compiled his evidence that he collected from the past, diaries and the like, into the form of that book. Your Honours have proofing notes, I think. The newspaper articles -- the witness has apparently said to the Prosecutors in -- in proofing that the there were some propaganda in these reports. Now, he says the book is devoid of propaganda, so the book is better than the -- the newspaper articles in that regard. I mean, the newspaper reports really do have this, in a sense -- it's difficult for the Defence, frankly. It puts us in a bad position. Do we cross-examine him about propaganda? I don't know. And how does it assist the Tribunal? But -- but then you've got in front of you newspaper articles written very much later. But coming to the book. The question is: In what way is it relevant? And in my submission, the danger of admitting that book or allowing the witness to use it at this instance is that it will replace his evidence. In other words that they'll be -- they'll be putting to evidence books -- newspaper -- I said about newspaper articles. They'll be put into evidence the book and -- and that that will become the evidence rather than the evidence of the witness himself. And once again, what my submission is is that the witness should give his account. He should say from the witness box in the normal way, like everyone else does, what it is that he saw and did. And that only after that, should it become necessary for some other reason, that that -- that be admitted into evidence. Now, as I say, the Prosecutor doesn't have to defend against an allegation that the material in there is relevant -- is irrelevant. Most of it is plainly relevant, and the objection is not as to relevance. But it is as to the using of those documents. In making the objection to the book and to the newspaper articles, I also want to mention that those -- both the book and the newspaper articles stand very much in the same position as statements made to investigators. All they really are accounts given by the witness on another occasion. In the first instance the witness should give his evidence here. If I should, for example, impugn the witness and say that "You've just made this up now. You've recently invented this," well, then of course those documents have a relevance and they could be admitted. In another situation, they may be relevant too, if the witness said, "Look, I cannot remember the date. I put it in my book. And when I put it in the book, I had good notes, so could I look at the book?" The Court might say, realistically speaking, "Of course you can." So it may be that those documents would have relevance. But in advance we don't know. We don't know what the witness is going to say. It might well be that he does remember and that he -- because he's obviously a person who has documented these matters and has been very closely involved, his actual memory is what the Court really needs to hear, what the Tribunal really needs to hear. And we don't place any limits on the relevant material that the Prosecution can lead and that's not what I'm objecting for now. It's the replacement of live evidence by -- by documentary evidence, which concerns me. And I say that -- and the final point I wish to make about that is this: That although this case has moved quickly, the fact is that it does take a number of weeks and memories of individual witnesses may be preserved and obviously experienced Judges do preserve those memories and you will. But at the same time, the documentary record will be important, and at the end of -- when you come to weigh up the testimony of this witness and you have in front of you his book, which is written in an easy to read journalistic style and you also have the transcript, which is peppered by my questions, potentially objections, and various other procedural things that happen, it is a task that the Tribunal doesn't need to have to discipline itself to read one part against the other part and to remember which part to rely on. Now, I'm not suggesting that you -- that the Tribunal can't do it. Of course you can. You do it all the time. But you don't need toe do it unless it's necessary, and it's distracting and time consuming and it may not be necessary. So those are the submissions about those documents. Turning on to -- now on to the book of -- from Halilovic. On the face of the materials that we have, there's just no basis for this witness to -- to -- to -- for that document to be tendered through this witness. Perhaps he's read it. Obviously the Prosecutors have read it. I've read it. Various people have read it. And so has this person and so possibly have other witnesses who are going to be called in the case. Now, that doesn't mean that it's -- that that witness is an appropriate person through whom to tender the document. And I've mentioned this before, that you will have noticed already that the Prosecutors have not called an investigator, and they're not -- there is no investigator on their list. Now, the normal course of events, of course, is that an investigator could be called to say, "Well, these are -- this is material that's been gathered through the investigation. We want to tender it through this -- this investigator." If the Defence has a quarrel or a dispute, then the Defence may raise a dispute about particular individual items and then proper proof may be required. But in this case, there is no investigator being called and we can't ask any questions about how the investigation proceeded, because there's no one to ask them of. And the Prosecutor obviously has its reasons for, and they're entitled to make their decisions about who they call and who they don't call. That's Prosecution strategy. But they can't have the benefit of not calling that witness and expect to have evidence just going in when there's no appropriate witness for it to go through. And this really appears, in my submission, to be an attempt to put a document into evidence, a document which this witness has no connection with whatsoever other than that he's read it. And it may be the evidence that he's read it for -- all -- part of it or all of it. But he's just not an appropriate witness to put it through. And therefore, I submit that that shouldn't be done, and I'd submit that before we start, therefore, in summary, the Prosecutor might be called upon to clarify what the situation is with the use of -- of Sanction concerning the audio transcript. That's the first thing. Secondly, the Prosecution may put any arguments that they have to raise concerning my submissions about this article and the book. And finally, the Prosecutor ought to indicate in advance why it is that this witness is an appropriate witness through whom to tender Sefer Halilovic's book or the extract of it which they wish to tender. And those are the matters that I wish to raise at this pre-trial stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that I have to give a chance to Ms. Chana to make some reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Counsel for the Defence has raised many points here, and I will start with the Sanction point. Your Honour, Ringtail cannot show audio. And that's the simple answer to that particular -- we're just going to show two minutes through Sanction because Ringtail apparently cannot -- you cannot have the voice, the audio in -- in Ringtail. We'll be happy to use Ringtail, if in fact Ringtail could actually do it. So that's the reason we're using Sanction, Your Honour. Now, secondly, I will deal with the -- the articles and the book that we intend to tender through Mr. Hodzic. Now, these are articles written by Mr. Hodzic himself, Your Honour, and whereupon he produced his book. These articles are written in 1999. It is only when the witness comes to court I will lay a foundation as to what was his memory, what was his sources, what was his journalistic style. But nevertheless, Your Honour, there are numerous precedents in the Tribunal where material produced by journalists has been admitted into evidence. Perhaps I may just refer to one case, one decision of the Appeals Chamber, where -- it's an authority to say that this is permissible. Your Honour, I've taken the liberty of making some copies for Your Honours and for the Defence of the decision of Brdjanin versus [sic] Talic, which is IT-99-36, and this is the Appeals decision on the 11th of December, 1999. Your Honour, we would -- we would argue that this is binding on this Chamber, since this is -- it's an Appeals decision. In that case, Your Honour, the Prosecution is thought to have an article written by a journalist admitted into evidence. The journalist himself was not present in court. The Appeals Chamber in that case recognised that because of public interest in accommodating the work of war correspondents, war correspondents enjoy certain privileges before the Tribunal and that in some cases this privilege may prevent a war correspondent from being subpoenaed to be cross-examined on an article that the journalist has written. However, Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber made it quite clear that even when it is not possible to call the journalist to be cross-examined on the accuracy of the article, it is still possible for the article to be admitted into evidence. The Appeals Chamber ruled that: "In this situation, the article is, however, hearsay and that the inability to cross-examine the journalist may go to the weight that the Trial Chamber would give it but does not mean that the article cannot be admitted as evidence." This, Your Honour, you will find at paragraph 52 of the decision. Your Honour -- Your Honours, in the present case, unlike in the Brdjanin and Talic case, the journalist is before the Trial Chamber. He can be cross-examined by the Defence on the accuracy of the material he has written, notwithstanding when he wrote it. So therefore, Your Honours, there are even stronger reasons for admitting this evidence -- this article and book into evidence. Your Honour, I -- we would argue there are also reasons why more weight should be given to it by the Trial Chamber. In short, therefore, Your Honour, the material written by the witness is admissible as evidence. It is a matter for Your Honours what weight to give it, and this question falls to be addressed by the parties in their final submissions at the end of the trial. Your Honour, the Defence have made no showing whatsoever how their client will be prejudiced by the admission of this material. Mr. Hodzic was the war correspondent. He was on the ground. He was privy to the events. He made notes. Even though he said some of it is propaganda, he will be asked whether the events, the dates, what he witnessed was accurate. And after laying the foundations, Your Honour, there'll be no question that this journalist wrote his articles and his book with the events that he himself witnessed. He can be cross-examined. Your Honour, there are no strict rules of admission of evidence at this Tribunal. It's a matter of relevance, probative value, and the question of weight Your Honours will give any particular evidence. So those would be my submissions in respect of admitting into evidence the articles and the book written by Mr. Hodzic. Your Honours, I intend to merely produce them into evidence. I am very mindful of the fact that there's limited time in calling this evidence. It is not meant to replace his evidence, Your Honour. He will be giving oral evidence. And therefore, it is by no means, as I -- as I indicated, as a replacement of his evidence, but the time will not allow him to give it as full a consideration as producing his articles, where Your Honours can see exactly in all the detail what he witnessed when he was a war correspondent on -- on the ground. Your Honours, the Defence alluded to -- to some motion that the Prosecution had filed and in the footnotes they said the articles cannot be deemed -- articles and newspaper cannot be deemed to be credible evidence. Your Honour, I would distinguish this case. These are not articles written by any other person. These are articles written by the journalist himself, and he is present in this court, and he can be asked any questions that the Defence deems appropriate to put to him. Your Honour, in respect of the book "Cunning Strategy" written by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Defence counsel does not argue it is irrelevant, which is quite appropriate, because it is extremely relevant. They say there's no connection between Mr. Halilovic's book and Mr. Hodzic. With due respect, Your Honour, I would disagree. There is a deep connection between the two. Halilovic, and the particular chapter that we wish to introduce into evidence -- Mr. Hodzic is deeply concerned with the events because he was there and he witnessed them. There is the connection, Your Honour, that Mr. Hodzic was with Mr. Halilovic during the course of Operation Neretva. He shadowed him most of the time, and he is also privy to the same events, which he witnessed to which Mr. Halilovic talks about. He is an extremely appropriate witness to have -- to talk about and assist the Chamber as to whether he finds the events as detailed by Mr. Halilovic in his book are to the best of his own knowledge and recollection accurate or not. Your Honour, this is a public publication. It's available to all in sundry. It's been published. It's open sources. And I do not again see the prejudice and there's been no showing of prejudice by the Defence as to why this would in any way inconvenience them, since it is open sources. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diary. Mr. Hodzic wrote his diary, and in respect of the diary, Your Honour, we're only going to be using some 10 lines of it, which is at the end of the diary. This is Mr. Hodzic's diary. And all my submissions in respect to the article and the books would apply in equal force when it comes to the diary. Your Honour, in this respect, these are my submissions. I hope I have not left any particular point out. Just other than to add that diaries are always admissible in -- in these proceedings, and I think the Defence counsel has conceded as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any short, very concise reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Always concise as possible, Your Honour. As to the question of the -- of the letters -- sorry, of the articles and the book, my learned friend really did reveal the true reason for doing this. She said there was pressure of time for this witness. And she said that she doesn't have the time to lead the evidence fully. And if you go back to page 13, line 19, you'll see. And what this is is exactly what I alluded to. It's an attempt toe replace the live testimony with this. It's an attempt to introduce a quasi 89(F) situation or a quasi-92 bis situation, whereby the written material goes in and then the Defence has the chance to cross-examine. That really is what it is. And my learned friend let the cat out of the bag and revealed that by referring to time, because that really is what the Prosecution is seeking to do, to replace the oral testimony with this material. Now, it may be at a later stage that this material has got relevance or assistance to give, but we don't want a trial where this material is handed up in lieu of the evidence. We want a trial where he gives his evidence. Your Honours, you will refer to the Brdjanin decision. That is absolutely irrelevant. That was a case concerning the privilege of journalists and whether they should be compelled to be called to be cross-examined about a -- about an article which was otherwise relevant and admissible. The real issue there was should the journalist be called. It had nothing to do with this situation. In this case, far from it assisting my friend's case, the real issue is that Mr. Hodzic is here. Let him say what he remembers. Let him say what happened. Should it be the case that he -- he has difficulties remembering, you might decide, depending on what he says, that he's allowed to refresh his memory from a particular document. But to put in the book as a replacement for his evidence is just not permissible, frankly, so I -- that's the submission I make in response to that. But I refer you to what my learned friend said at page 13 on line 19 and following, and you'll see what it is that she said in justification for her argument. It's quite plainly an attempt to put this evidence in as evidence, and the Prosecutor never did say to you it's the live evidence that counts and this material has some other function or some supplementary function. The Prosecutor is trying to use it as evidence, and they shouldn't be permitted to. We should hear from Mr. Hodzic. You might decide something different later, but give him a chance. He's a witness. He's come to The Hague. That's what we want to hear. I'll turn to the question of -- of the admissibility of the book of Halilovic. The Prosecutor's argument came down to this: That Mr. Hodzic was there at the same time. That's what the argument was. Mr. Hodzic has a very clear interest in this book, the Prosecutor said, because he was there. Your Honours, every single witness called from the crime scene situation may be the -- subject to the same comment. Witness D apparently was there. Would it have been appropriate to put this book in through Witness D? That cannot be a basis and that's the only basis that's being advanced here. So in my submission, that must fail. As to the diary issue, frankly, my friend is quite right about that and really the clarification there, so long has it's a contemporaneous diary, of course, that would be exactly the sort of document that the witness should be allowed to refer to fresh his memory, and quite frankly I don't know why they're limiting it down to -- to the two minutes, because it's -- it's relevant. But those are what I have to say in reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we spent about 35 minutes to debate on this issue. But as a matter of fact, even before the start of this case, this Bench has issued a ruling concerning with the guidelines of -- of the admission of the evidence. I hope both parties could find the time to discuss all -- or carefully read whatever is said in that decision. During the whole proceedings, as the Defence counsel rightly pointed out, that the best-evidence rule should be the guidance of this trial, that is, if we have a live witness giving testimony in the proceedings, so I believe that his testimony will be the best evidence because those evidence was tested by the cross-examination of the other party. This is the rule that we have to abide by. As for the other matters, I believe that the submissions by the Defence is confused with two different categories of matters: One is the using of this document in the proceedings; the other is the admission of this document into the evidence. As the Bench pointed before, that so long as that document is relevant, it is important for the party introducing this document to prove its case, and so long as there are some probative value and those documents are usable in the proceedings. As for how much weight the Bench should put to those documents and whether think should be admitted into the evidence, I believe those matters should be discussed after we heard that witness's testimony, because the Defence counsel has the full right to challenge the admission of that document by cross-examination or by putting some questions to the witness. So in this way, I believe that at this stage the tape, the book, the articles, as well as the diary, are usable through this witness in the proceedings. As for whether those documents are admissable or not, we'll leave it to the end of the proceedings. It is so decided. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please give your name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Sefko Hodzic. I was born on the 28th of November, 1945.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I'm a journalist, a journalist in Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been a journalist at the Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I've been working for Oslobodjenje for the past 15 years, and the other 20 years I've been working for other media, newspapers and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all in all, you've been a journalist for how many years, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: About 35 or 36 years. Perhaps it would have been better if it was a little less, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell this Chamber your academic background.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I am a teacher of literature, and I completed the Faculty of Philosophy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year would this be?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also work for Radio Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I worked there in a professional capacity in 1974 -- 1973.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you won any awards for your journalism?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I received a prize by the Association of the Journalists of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also received the Oslobodjenje annual award which we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year was this, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: This Oslobodjenje award I received in 1996. And as for the other one, I really don't know. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in 1994 and 1995 nominated for the best reporter of the year?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was declared the war correspondent of the year, and this was an award I shared with a colleague. In 1994 and 1995, I was in the finals - we could put it like that - for that award.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you a war correspondent in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1993 and all the war years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, you were working for the Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a journalist employed in Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many other reporters were reporting during the war, from the field?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: In the first months of 1992, there were many. And then the numbers kept dwindling, so that only a few of us remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did these numbers dwindle, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I know that my colleagues from Oslobodjenje - I wasn't the only war correspondent from Oslobodjenje - some of them fled abroad; some of them were afraid; they couldn't bring themselves to go to the front any more, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you persevered.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you would send your reports to Sarajevo. What was the methodology of reporting?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Exclusively -- actually, not exclusively. There were some phones -- well, in Sarajevo, I went to the offices. I either wrote from home or went to the news room. But when I was outside of Sarajevo, there were some phone lines somewhere, so I was able to fax in my report. But the most usual way was to use the ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were out in the field during Operation Neretva, how would you send your reports back?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Exclusively through ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which communications centre did you mostly use?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The communications centre of the 44th Mountain Brigade in Jablanica. On two occasions, from this part, from the power station, I sent it out from there. For some reason this location was referred to as the IKM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would receive your reports?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There was some sort of schedule there. I think the person who responded had a -- a code name, Zoka. All the ham radio operators knew each other. I don't know where they were located, but they would receive the reports and they would send them on to our centre, which we also had at Oslobodjenje. We had a communications centre. It would be received by the centre, retyped by our typist. Since from 1993, at the request of people from Radio Sarajevo, I was allowed by my editor-in-chief to work for them as well, to work for the radio as well, so at the same time my reports were used by Oslobodjenje and by the radio, the radio of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your -- your articles would find their way in the newspaper and there would be a radio programme. Would this be every day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you couldn't say that it was every day, but specially in 1992 and 1993. I was very busy. You could say that. You couldn't say it was every day, but it was quite frequent. I would go to the front, most often to Zuc, where the combat operations were going on. I would report in for 1500 hours, 1700 hours. Then I would go to the news room, work until 11.00. I would develop the photographs, and then they would be published the next day in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the date and location always indicated on your reports?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Only if I forgot something. But my first thing was always to put the date in and then take notes. When I was working for the radio, when I was recording the material into the microphone, then I would usually say I want. Sometimes I would make a mistake. I would skip it. But I would say, "Today is" -- then I would say the date, "I am at such-and-such a location." And then I would speak with the fighters and the commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how accurate was the information in respect of dates and places in your reports? How accurate was that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Sometimes there were mistakes. I would catch some mistakes, especially during those first years of the war. And I wouldn't know the date or what day it was. That would happen sometimes. It would seem to me that it was one date but then later I would go back and see that it was actually another day. I would correct these mistakes later when I checked when these articles were published in Oslobodjenje. If it was published on the 25th, then it must mean that I had sent it in on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why is it that you are -- you were clear about dates?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I was clear about it. I used different ways. But mostly based on my notes from the war. I kept most of them; although, some of the pages are torn. When I went out on a trip, I received travel orders from the news room, and then I would specify exactly how many days I was away, where I was, how long I stayed. The first page of the report would always contain the travel orders for Igman, for the Operation Neretva. I would usually state that. So that's the documentation that I kept, and I still have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it also the case, Mr. Hodzic, that you were given allowances by Oslobodjenje and you had to put in the returns, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't object to the witness giving evidence, but I do object to there being leading of the witness and putting propositions to him like that. And I want to be clear that I'll object like that throughout if there's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this situation, I don't believe that it's quite leading. I believe that the Prosecution has to lead the witness in certain subjects or areas. Otherwise, we'll never be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's quite true. And the witness is entitled to say what he has to say about the topic and not have the proposition put to him by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, was there any particular reason as to why the dates were quite clear to you? Were there anything else, any other administration which made you remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: As I said, as far as this operation is concerned and the one at Igman -- actually, for Igman, I had more documents because there was fighting every day, so I took notes every day. But as I said, this report, the one for Igman and Neretva, I put together. It was one report. We would receive 500 German marks a day -- no, no, no, we received 50 German marks a day, but only when Oslobodjenje received a donation of this money from other sources. But sometimes I wouldn't receive any advance allowance. For example, when I went to cover the Neretva operation, I didn't receive anything. I would only receive this money when I came back. Sometimes even six months would pass before I would actually be paid these allowances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have to put in some paperwork to claim these allowances.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, not then or now. You only submit a report. Along with the travel orders, you only have to submit your hotel or accommodation bills. That would be the only thing. I would have to submit a bill for the hotel, and this would be paid on top of the allowance. But there would be no other expenses other than the travel expenses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hodzic, you said you would write the articles. And when you wrote the articles, would you please tell us the sources of your information. How would you -- what were the -- the sources of your information as you wrote those articles? What would you rely on?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Out in the theatre, I would report as an eyewitness. My articles were not any sort of pieces of wisdom. I would speak to the fighters, with the commanders, take photographs, and describe what I saw, what I experienced. So it was conveying my direct experiences in the theatre of war and what happened. That's what I would put in the articles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make notes?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have about 120 or 150 of these different volumes of notes that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you wrote your book. How many books have you written altogether to date, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I published some things, but what's relevant for this now is that I published four books about the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote your books, where did the information come from?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It depends on the book. The first one is about the reports straight from the front. I just corrected some minor mistakes, and it was just published like that. The third book is the one that's here now. It's sort of three or four longer, broader pieces. I was a participant, and I also reported about Neretva, and I don't know what else is in there. But this was not based only on my recollections. I was lucky enough that the commanders, General Delic and General Dudakovic allowed me to use archival material, so I was allowed access to the archives and I used that material, and I incorporated that into my writing, and I also spoke to people who directly participated in the events. So it was my testimony, the testimony of those who directly participated, plus archive material that -- that went into the third book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that this accords with the highest journalistic standards? Would you say that to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I kept to that during the war as much as I could. Of course there was some mistakes. These were not intentional mistakes. They happened, but always my objective was to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the time you wrote the book, did you correct some of the -- the mistakes and the dates in the articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm just not sure the witness has said anything about mistakes and dates of articles at all in this court at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought the witness had said that other than a few mistakes on the dates, everything was accurate, but I will put it again to -- to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, he said there was no intentional mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, can you -- can you let -- could you please assist the Chamber by telling them how many mistakes had you made in respect of dates and how many were there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: In relation to this topic here, I established that there had been only one mistake relating to the dates, and that's the date when I met with Mr. Sefer Halilovic in Konjic. I don't know where I made the mistake, but in the statement, in the book, and in the long piece I wrote that we met on the 22nd of August, and Mr. Sefer Halilovic gave a pass for my mother for the tunnel on that occasion. When I looked at the archives a while ago, I found out -- I saw that it said the 23rd there, but then I cross-checked my notes from that area, and then when I saw when the consultations were in Zenica, then I saw that it was actually on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other mistake, to your knowledge, on the date, other than the one you've just described?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps there were, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Hodzic, I'd like you to see your articles and if you would please identify them?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is 65 ter number 126. And I will read out the number: 03423148.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are your articles, Mr. Hodzic, from 15 January to 6 February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it would be easier if I just showed Mr. Hodzic all the articles to identify them, because I'm not going to do any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, before that's done, I raise this issue, that -- bearing in mind Your Honours' ruling, these documents are completely permissible, but the witness should be given the chance to give his evidence first before we come to these -- these documents. He's here. It's a live trial. And -- I have no objection to the witness looking at them. I have no doubt he's seen them many times. But in terms of the evidence that's to be led, whilst you may permit him to look at the articles, he really has to be given the chance to say what -- what he recalls, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Are we still talking about the mistakes in those dates?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'll merely mark them for identification at this stage and then I'll produce them -- it's just that -- I want to now to identify the articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask some preliminary questions on this article. For instance, what the contents are about, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the articles that the usher is showing you, please. What are these articles, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a series of articles that I wrote for Oslobodjenje as of the 15th of January, 1993 about Neretva 93, and there was a subheading "Witness of the Operation Neretva," 23 installments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they all on Operation Neretva, or is there any other matter included on those articles?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: All of them. Well, basically all of them, but then I based it on my memories of other things in relation to that. For example, I wrote about the Igman operation, which was a month earlier, because some of the same persons were cropping up there. So there are some other things there, but there are certain serious errors there, because I was basing this account on my notes, and I went to the radio station and they gave to me some of the cassettes that they had kept, because I hadn't kept them. And there are some mistakes there, especially when I based my account on my memories. There were some errors that had crept in. But most of these errors were actually corrected in the book. There are possible errors here, but there are no mistakes in the book that I can think of because I tried to correct all of those when I was writing the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these the -- the articles that you sent from the field as you were in the field as a war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did use the articles because this is something I wrote in January 1999, and then I was using the articles that I wrote in 1993 and accounts and the reports for the radio. Some things I couldn't even find any more. And of course I based it all on the way I remembered these things. But not on the basis of any documents. Maybe I did have a couple of documents, but I can't remember. I don't think so. But basically without any archives, any documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were based on the reports you sent from the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Your Honours, just -- sorry. I apologise to the witness. When I interrupt it's to make a legal objection. Your Honours, there's two things to say: The first one is that that's a plainly leading question. And secondly, it's a -- really flies in the face of what -- of the answers that the witness had already given. Now, I've got no objection to my learned friend just asking the normal questions about when he filed reports, what he relied upon to -- to -- to build up the articles and then how he corrected those articles when he came to write the book, which I think is what the witness is -- is heading to say. Given Your Honours' rulings, that's not objectionable. But it's just got to be done in a step by step way and not to put things in the witness's mouth, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that it is a leading question, but in some situations the leading question is allowed, and in this particular matter, it does not go to the actual conduct of the crime. It's just to establish the source of this article. But anyway, Ms. Chana, maybe you could put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm obliged to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, what were these 1999 articles based upon?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, my articles were based on reports, daily reports that I sent in from Herzegovina for both the radio and Oslobodjenje, and they were also based on my notes, the notes I'd kept. And I think I kept one or two cassettes and some other materials. And on my memory in fact, basically. And I also consulted some other sources, such as Bilajac and Karic and Suljevic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would mark it for identification. And that's number 288, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hodzic, I would like to now show you 65 ter number 183, Your Honour, which is 01062078.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I believe these will be shown on Ringtail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, this is some excerpts from your book. And I'm sorry, even if I try, I will not be able to pronounce the Bosnian version, but I think it is "The unsealed envelope." Now, they will come up before the screen, Mr. Hodzic, and if you'd just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may explain. These are certain -- from -- from Mr. Hodzic's book. And we have the ERN range and we have just translated only certain portions of Mr. Hodzic's book, and those are the only portions that we wish to tender into evidence. And I would now like the witness to identify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see what's on the screen, Mr. Hodzic, and would you tell us what is it? Perhaps if you could go page by page. I mean, I think that's where, I think, e-court system false short, Your Honour, that ...

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a heading. It is translated properly, the title of the book. And this is one of the installments, which is "The last supper at ARK."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, can we just -- Your Honour, I don't know if there's a simpler way of doing this so that the witness can actually see all of the -- the pages so that we can save some time. Otherwise, this will take a very long time for us to go page by page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Mr. Halilovic can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that you agree that this document could be furnished to this witness in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any objection at all to the witness being furnished it. And frankly, I can't see why he's -- why it's been chopped up in the way it has. I don't have any objection to the witness just being given his whole book to look at. He wrote it. And we're not going to require that he have each little passage put to him. It's obvious he wrote it, and it's -- he's entitled to give that evidence. My friend can actually lead on that. I just make the point I'm -- I'm struggling to see why these little segments are taken out. But that's the Prosecution's decision. If they want to persist with it, I suppose they can. I don't object to leading on whether those article -- those items were written by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Defence, Your Honours, for that indication. And the reason why only certain parts have been translated, Your Honour, is that it's a translation issue, and we're mindful of Your Honours' ruling at some point where you did not want whole -- whole books tendered into evidence, so we thought we would only translate the relevant portions so as not to burden the Court with too much material, Your Honour. And we have really highlighted only the relevant portions. But we can show the witness his entire book in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I'm going to give you a hard copy of this. And if you followed what I said to Their Honours earlier on, what -- what this is is sections of your book which actually I have -- the Prosecution has translated. Would you look at this book and -- and confirm that it is indeed your book. If you'd look at the -- the hard copy in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's rather obvious. We are talking about a paragraph from my book "Sealed envelope," which -- "The unsealed envelope," - sorry - which refers to this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, could you tell us: When you wrote this book, what did you base the information on?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that already. I mean, if you want me to repeat, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You -- you said they were the articles. I would like now for you to tell us about this book and the sources of your information on the book.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that's from the book. So that's the book. The book has been complemented by the documents that I had, by the series of articles that I had published and that you have shown me a while ago, and it has been complemented by extra documents pertaining to the Neretva operation that I obtained from the archives. And in the meantime, I've also used some UNPROFOR materials. I looked through the press, Oslobodjenje, from that particular period. And I also talked to some people, Arif Pasalic, et cetera. And so it was all complemented on the basis of the new information on the new documents and I apologise for asking you to repeat the question. I hadn't quite understood what you were getting at in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite all right, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this book, MFI289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But what is the title of this book?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, I thought he'd said it. Would you please tell Their Honours what the title of your book is.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The title of the book is "The unsealed envelope," and the heading for this paragraph is "The Witness of Operation Neretva," but the title does not come from there but the title is based on another operation, which is called Operation Envelope, and I also wrote that on the basis of archives, et cetera, but it was a kind of mystery novel. And so the operation was called "Envelope" so I established this kind of link, an unsealed envelope, so that's -- that's it basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. But the documents received don't have this translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, we have translated it into English, Your Honour. It was done just a few days ago. It hasn't been something which has been in the system for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But we can always -- we always had it in B/C/S, but we can always provide Your Honours with the -- the -- I think Ram is nodding that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hodzic, I would like you, if you would, to cast your mind to 9th June 1993. Could you tell us what you did on that day.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the 9th -- or on the 8th of June, the news was broadcast that there had been some changes in the army and the editor-in-chief -- that is to say, that Sefer Halilovic was where he was and the commander-in-chief was Rasim Delic. And the editor-in-chief asked me -- he called me on the phone and he said, "Can you write something about this new commander? Can we have a presentation of this guy?" And I said, "I've never heard of him myself." And so all we published were these bare facts from the Presidency of the government about the latest changes in the government. And then in the morning I was asked by the editor-in-chief to go to the Chief of Staff and to take a photographer with me, because we didn't even have his photo. And we were also going to ask for a statement and a statement to the effect about the distribution of tasks and competencies if Sefer remained where he was and now he's a new commander and we tried to find out what it was all about. And I went early in the morning to Mr. Sefer Halilovic's office, and they were changing the system. It was an official ceremony and there was a General Muslimovic and I asked him to try and find out whether the commander was ready to receive us, whether we could take his photo, and whether he could make a statement. And only Sefer and Delic stayed there and Sefer's people told me that Sefer wanted to resign because he was told by somebody else half an hour earlier that he was going to be replaced, et cetera. And then I was told, "The commander is waiting for you." And I went in and I stayed with Delic. I -- what I had in mind was a photo opportunity and a brief statement. But then we stayed longer and we had a talk. And one of the questions was about the distribution of competencies, and I did ask other questions as well, but one of the questions was about these changes. And he said that it was all well known what the competencies were because he had published this interview in his book. And then I included it in my book. And he said, "We knew what the Chief of Staff was supposed to do but basically the commander has the last word." And then Sefer came along again, and I asked him about the resignation, and he said, "No," and then I asked Delic, "Did he really hand in his resignation?" "No, no, no." And then he used the formal words. I can't remember whether he said, "There are too many Sefers" or "Sefer is one and only." Or something like that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I believe that you are eager to give your evidence, but whatever you said has to be recorded into the transcript, so please go very slowly so that the interpreter and typewriter could follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. I was going to say exactly the same to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, if you'd please listen to His Honour Judge Liu. Go a little slower. Otherwise, it becomes extremely difficult for the interpreter. And I would ask the interpreter to please actually themselves indicate that to the witness. So you interviewed Delic and -- and you talked about Mr. Halilovic's general demeanour about it. When was it that Delic was made the -- the Supreme Commander of the army? What date was it? When he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He was appointed -- no, that was published on the 8th. The Presidency made the decision about the appointment of Rasim Delic. He had not been a general at that time. And it was a new job which did not exist before, and Sefer Halilovic stayed in his previous job, which was the Chief of Staff. And we did not talk a great deal about Sefer at all. And I asked him whether it was true that he had handed in his resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would -- why would Sefer Halilovic want to resign?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I was told by his people whilst I was waiting for the commander to see me, "He is going to hand in his resignation. This is not fair behaviour." At the eleventh hour they told him that he -- that there was going to be somebody new. And then when he came again himself, when I was with Delic already, I asked him, "Are you going to hand in your resignation?" And he said, "When the time comes, I'll let people know." And then Delic went on to say what I've said before, that he didn't have any information about that. And I think he said something like, "Sefer is one and only and there aren't too many people like Sefer," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take a photograph of Delic and Sefer together?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. There was a photographer there, because I did not have a camera myself. And there was a rather interesting situation there: When Sefer came in to say something and Delic was sitting across the table from me and we were talking and then Sefer was bringing something in to Delic and asking him something, and I thought it would be a nice image, as it were, that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I'm going to have to interrupt you. It becomes very difficult to follow you, Mr. Hodzic. If you could really make an effort to slow down.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I know. You'll have to tell me again, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: So as I was saying, Sefer was standing and it was a rather symbolic image of this change. So Delic was sitting down. Sefer was standing up behind him. And I asked the photographer, "Take this picture. That's great." And then he was grabbing his camera and Sefer said, "No," and Delic said nothing. And I thought it would be a shame for such a symbolic image not to be captured on film, but no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to be photographed together?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't really refuse. He -- I don't know. I mean -- well, I don't know. I mean, there was nothing nasty about it. I -- I mean, he didn't like being photographed in general, so I didn't take it as a formal rejection. Or he didn't like to give statements either. I once talked to his head of cabinet. We see more of the Pope in the press and in the media rather than your guys there and there is a war in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now I'll take you to 23rd August 1993. Can you tell me who you met on that day, if anybody at all?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I gave a detailed account of those events in the book. I went down for a five-day period as a reporter from Mostar with a group of people from Mostar. I found out that my birthplace, Razici, had fallen and it is a part of the Konjic area, and I separated from the group. They went on to Mostar and I myself went on to that mountain area because I had heard about refugees. My mother was there. I found my mother and I went back to Konjic after five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: And I think it was the most difficult situation I found myself in during the war. What was I supposed to do? I had to go to Mostar. I couldn't leave my mother. She didn't want to leave me. I went to Sarajevo. I talked to Bilajac. He said nobody other than Sefer and Delic can give you permission to travel through the tunnel with your mother. Civilians are not supposed to go. It's a no-go area. I could go. The army could go. But civilians couldn't go. I was in a very difficult situation. I didn't know what to do. And that's what had happened. At a certain point, on Monday, I set out and I was staying with some relations near Konjic with my mother and we set out in the direction of Konjic and there was a jeep driving by and I saw Zuka at the wheel and Sefer was asleep in the passenger seat. So, well, this a bingo for me, a million dollars. A win at the lottery. I was so pleased to see him. And I went in the area where the 6th Corps was. I thought that that was what they were headed for. And he was there and Karavelic and Zuka and many other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I noticed Sefer. He was up there. And he saw me, and we went towards one another and they were all in a good mood and Karavelic came and I said, "Sefer, you are my favourite person on earth right now." And he said, "Why?" And then I told him the story. And he said, "Well, I've got --" and I said, "Well, I've got my mother here. I don't know what to do with her." And he said, "Look, I've got the stamp and everything. I'm going to stamp all the papers for you and I'll sign the document and a pass for your mother so that she can travel," et cetera. And he wrote on a piece of paper, "I'm asking all the heads of units to help this person out."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did Sefer give you this -- this pass? What else did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He gave me -- no, I said to him and he said, "What are you -- where are you going?" And I told him the whole story. And then I said to him, "Okay. I was on my way to Mostar and Santic, Ulica, and the Bulevar were the symbolic streets as far as the defence of Mostar was concerned and I said I was on my way to Mostar to report about the Santic, Ulica, and the Bulevar. And he said to me, "I am myself -- was on my way to Mostar. I'm going to be in Mostar pretty soon but in a slightly different way. We are preparing to lift the blockade of Mostar," and he said either that Bilajac, Zicro Suljevic, Karic -- either he said they were already there or they were preparing to go down there, and then he said, "I'm going to be going down there as well and I'm going to be leading this operation." And that's when I asked him, "Dear Sefer, let me go with you. Let me send my mother back to Sarajevo and let us go happily -- well, not happily, but unburdened of all my worries," and then he said, "Oh, okay. Yes." And so I came back. But what I had in mind going to Mostar and what I was basically ordered to do by my boss, I couldn't do it because of that unexpected situation involving my mother. I had to go back to Sarajevo. And then we agreed we would set out together, when he would -- decided to go to Mostar. And I called him several times. We were in touch basically in order to arrange our trip together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when he said, "We are going to Mostar," what did you understand who this "we" encompassed?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: You mean in Konjic or where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, you just said that Sefer said to you, "We are going to lift the blockade of Mostar." Who is this "we"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Us, the Army of the BH, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'll take you to 31st August. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, on that day and the days before, I phoned him every day and he said, "I'll let you know when we can go," and then I called him up again and he said, "Come to my place at 8.00 this evening."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: That meant that I should pack up. And I packed my suitcase. I was living in a part of town -- I went out into the street waiting for some form of transport because I -- there were not many vehicles. And all of a sudden there was a car, which stopped next to me, and I looked in and Sefer was there with his people, and they were driving by there by chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was with Sefer with -- in this car?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea. Some people. Some of the escorts and perhaps a woman as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. He had a chauffeur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went to his -- at the headquarters, and I left my journalist's gear there, and he asked me to wait a little bit longer, and I went out and I went for a walk in town. And quite by chance I met with his friend and colleague from the Patriotic League. He was not a general as yet, Kemo Karisika, and he said that he was going down there as well and he was going to the officers' school in Zenica. And then I went back to his place and I think it was about 9.00 when we set out, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you set out? You left Sarajevo, is that right, at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps even at 10.00. I can't remember. So we -- his and I left his office and went through the tunnel. We never stopped. And we -- there was a jeep waiting for us there. Somebody called Mesar was driving. And we went to the IKM of the 1st Corps in Hrasnica and Kemo came by as well and we had a conversation there, and at one point we drove down to Herzegovina. And when we went to Konjic and Kemo went with his people, his professors and us, and I don't know what we were looking for, perhaps for Slavko Gusic. But we went to the 6th Corps. I can't remember whether we found him or not. And then we -- Karisika went to Zenica and we went to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I'm going to take you through the events step by step, so if you would assist me in doing that. You said there was a chap called Mesar. Where was Mesar from? Who was Mesar?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Mesar. Mesar. He was the driver. When I used to drive with Mr. Sefer, he would be the driver. I don't know if anybody else drove Mr. Sefer, but whenever I rode with Mr. Sefer, he was the one who drove the jeep. Later I found out this was a person from Sandzak. His name was Elmedin Causevic. All the people from Sandzak could conceal their names. I don't know for what reason. But his nickname was Mesar. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, just before the break, was he a soldier and from what unit was he?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Mesar was a fighter in Zuka's unit, and a month before that I met him at Igman, when the Serbian forces under the direct command of Mladic were attacking Igman and Bjelasnica. So I saw him operating a three-barrelled weapon. He was a little bit pale, and that's -- that's how I saw him. And that's when I met him for the first time. We talked a little bit and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, before we continue, I will remind you, please, if you would speak slowly, because the interpreters have to interpret everything you say and everyone has asked me to -- to indicate this to you so that -- you have some very valuable information, and we want to be quite sure that Their Honours are not straining to understand you. Now, before the break, Mr. Hodzic, you had just said that you went through the tunnel and you were met by somebody from Zuka's unit. Now, this is -- we are still on the 1st of September. And where did you go on the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went to Jablanica. We arrived at about 6.30, perhaps a little bit earlier. Sefer -- we went on to Donja Jablanica, where the base of the Zulfikar unit was, and we stayed there. One of his escorts, by the name of Sefko Halilovic, we stayed there, him and me. We got a room. And when we came out, that's when Sefer told me -- we were coming out of the car. He was coming out, and he said, "Sefko, we're here. You do your job and I will do mine." I didn't understand then what he meant. I only understood it later, because actually he didn't want - and I didn't ask him to - for me to attend any of their military meetings. So I didn't do that. He returned to Jablanica, and we stayed in Donja Jablanica. Later I found out that he spent the night at Zuka's. I often came to this apartment of Zuka where he was staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you have a conversation with Sefer Halilovic as to what his role in the operation was?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We mostly talked, and I kind of prompted that kind of conversation about the Patriotic League, which I was preoccupied with for a time and in which he was the number-one person, as well as Kemo Karisik. We also talked about the Owen-Stoltenberg plan. He was also obsessed with that in the same way that I was obsessed with the Patriotic League, about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three republics. That's when the most intense talks were, about the division. At that time, he told me that in Zenica they had agreed that Bosnia would not be divided. This was at the military meeting there. What his differences were on that with President Alija Izetbegovic -- well, that was mostly what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his role, Mr. Hodzic, what did he -- how did he see his own role and how did you see it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I still didn't know. He for me was still the Chief of Staff, as he had been always. I didn't know what the relationships were. As far as I was concerned, Sefer Halilovic was commander. Sefer Halilovic, who from the start was the embodiment right from when he was appointed commander ever commander. Although he had been a commander for only a month, he still was commander to me, even though he became the Chief of Staff. All the fighters and I thought of him still as commander. Even my deputy editor-in-chief, a woman who had written a poem on page 1 of Oslobodjenje, and the title of the poem was "He komandant," "Hey commander," even though he wasn't a commander any more. For me, I liked him as much as I did before we had a good personal relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was he perceived in the -- in the area by other army officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: They were happy to see him there amongst them. The people that we saw there were very happy that he was there. Both the fighters and the people were feeling somewhat abandoned. Sarajevo was a centre, and it was a bit separate. It seemed as if they were even happy to see me and not just Sefer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you wrote your reports, how did you refer to Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I didn't mention him at all.
