Later I identified him in the following way: He was the commander, regardless of anything; and when he said that he was going to be leading the operation, to me that was as if he were the commander of the operation. I had an image of him as Commander Sefer who was managing or conducting -- heading this operation. So as far as I was concerned, he was a commander. Later when we talked, it turned out that it wasn't quite the same to command or to direct an operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, in 1993, when you were writing this report that you referred to him as "commander," did -- did Mr. Halilovic ever correct you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wrote the reports. He didn't know when I was sending them and where I was sending them to. The first time I called him "commander" was in a kind of euphoric moment, on the 19th of September, when we found out that Medvjed had been liberated and when it looked as if the operation will be successful and when all the plans that had been made, it looked as if they would be achieved. When we were at Adnan Solakovic's base in Jablanica and when Zuka informed us that Medvjed had been taken and five times as much territory, we were euphoric. We were a little bit irrational. I spoke to everybody, and I'm sorry I that I didn't keep that raw tape so you could see what the atmosphere was like for yourself. That was the first time when I said -- well, I really said "coordinator," because he said to me, "It's one thing what I called him and it's another thing what he told me." The first time I went there and when I asked him and Karic, "What is your role here," and I took a paper, and you have this paper here in my notebook. I said, "What are you, Sefer?" And I wrote down, "Sefer," and he said, "I am a coordinator," and I wrote down "coordinator of the operation." And you have that. But how shall I put it? It was the first time I heard that a coordinator existed. Fighting was being conducted. So in my opinion, it was ridiculous to call him "coordinator." So in some instances I said that he was controlling, and in some instances I said that he was commanding the operation. I said in that report, "Sefer, who is coordinating," and that wasn't enough, so I said -- well, "and commanding." So he was there. I don't remember him saying anything to the contrary. Perhaps other people would remember, but perhaps he thought Well, since all this joyful -- this joyful mood was prevailing, well, he might have thought Well, I'll just let it go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 1st of September, Mr. Hodzic, did you go to Igman's Wolves in Grabovica at the hydroelectric plant?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all went: Sefer, Zuka, Bilajac, Karic, the whole crew. Zuka was there, and Nihad, and we all went to that unit, the Igman Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see some detainee there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any detainees. A little bit earlier, to the left in the prefab huts -- well, before the visit, we went to the huts where the freed inmates, Bosniaks who had been in Croat camps in Herzegovina, were situated, and we spoke to them. Sefer, Karic, we were all together. I took photographs. I spoke to those people. And then from there we went to the Igman Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the refugees talk to you and Sefer and the others about the way they had been treated in Croatian camps?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Of course. They were telling us all kinds of things. They were exhausted. I took photographs of them, and you can see that, and very soon after I -- I wrote an article or a -- a piece about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hodzic, I'll take you straight to 3rd September, if I may. Could you tell us on that day what you did.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It's specific in the book, but please don't hold me to everything. I may not remember everything. On the 3rd of September, I think we, Sefer Halilovic, Zuka, and their escort and myself, I think we went to a -- a sort of resort for rich people from Mostar in some mountain. I don't know what it's called. At the time, I didn't know what kind of an accommodation it was. But anyway, when we got there, Zuka mentioned it -- at the time, I didn't even know any Sarajevo units were coming. Zuka mentioned something about accommodation for some fighters. And in the beginning I thought Zuka wants to billet some of his fighters. We passed through Grabovica, went through that forest. We went up there somewhere. I don't know where we went. And they were looking around. I heard them speaking that it would be possible to billet them here. To me it seemed that that wasn't possible. Everything was damaged. And then we returned and -- and we went to Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to be clear about, this what was the exact purpose about you, Zuka, and Halilovic going to, as you said, this -- I don't know exactly what you -- you said you went through Grabovica to this resort. What was the purpose of -- of the three of you setting off on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: At the time, I understood it as if Zuka was looking for accommodation for his fighters. We passed through this forest and we went to this mountain resort which was all destroyed, and that's how I understood it. Well, since I wrote it five years later, in the book I didn't want to say what I thought and then what I found out later, I wrote that this was actually meant to be for the accommodation of the fighters from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, no, we passed through Grabovica, went through the forest, went out of Grabovica. There was a forest. There were some minefields that were marked. We were afraid, whether we can go in or not, but then we still go in, then went further up, and then went to reach this kind of weekend settlement where these little forest homes were. And then we were there for a while, and then we returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, when you went through Grabovica, what did you see in Grabovica? What -- what was it? What kind of a village was it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I could see that there was some elderly women and men there. There were people wearing black or longer folk costume. But anyway, there were some special caps and things. I could just tell by looking at them that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said you went to this forest. Did you stop the car at any point?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We stopped the car before we actually entered this holiday camp because minefields were marked, so that's where we went out. And Mesar was standing there thinking, Do we dare go in or not, and then Semir -- Sefer said, "Well, we won't know until we do it. If we are fated to die, then so be it." So we went in and then we went up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go next and what was this place where you went?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The place is called Kostajnica. Kostajnica or Neretvica. Kostajnica, Neretvica, Buturovic Polje. This is a broader area. It has different names. But Kostajnica was the actual place, or Neretvica. That's where the command of the 44th Brigade is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you get to Kostajnica, you -- I'm asking about this holiday chalet - is that what you called it - that you went to? Where was that? Where you thought it was not suitable for accommodation. I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We didn't think that. They determined that it was suitable, that it was possible. The roofs were intact. Zuka thought that it would be a good place for their accommodation. The housing was quite adequate. It's a place -- to get to it, you go through the forest, and then you go through the forest again. The road forks off to the left and then again goes through the forest. And then there were these minefields that we passed through. For hunters generally, from hunters from Mostar, this was -- this was where the president -- I mean, the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Dzemal Bijedic used to come very frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the place called, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It's called Diva Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then after this reconnaissance, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Without stopping, we returned to the village of Kostajnica, the municipality in Konjic. This is the municipality where I'm from. I was with Sefer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find any people there that you -- that you all met?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: As soon as we got to Kostajnica in the car, as soon as we came out of the car, a whole bunch of people gathered around us, women, children, elderly people. There were also people from the military units, from the local commune. They all gathered around Sefer. They started to complain to him. They started to threaten. There were about 20 elderly Croats in that village, and later on that day I spoke with them and I wrote an article about them, about these elderly Croats that had stayed. Sefer then started to say something to them. I turned my tape recorder on and Sefer said, "No, no, please -- please don't. Don't do it now." Then chaos erupted around him. They started to complain, and everything -- and I did switch my tape recorder on. It wasn't a Dictaphone. It was a radio -- it was a nice tape recorder which I got from the radio station with a nice microphone. You could tape the conversations of our fighters in Zuc and the Serbian fighters. So I -- I turned on this tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Sefer Halilovic say?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Since there was some threats in relation to the Croats who stayed there, he said, "No, no, no. But they kept interrupting him. It's very precise in the book. He said, "We're not a revengeful army. No woman should have to cry because of us. We're fighting against Chetniks and Ustashas." This is what he was saying, "And not -- and we will win," something to that effect. And then some women supported what he was saying, and then he said, "Don't cry. No woman [as interpreted] won a war by attacking women and children." He said something to the effect that no woman or no child should be made to cry. They mustn't be attacked. And I called that "the ethics of Sefer's warfare." That was how I titled that in my book. And I literally retyped -- I transcribed everything from the tape as he was being interrupted and everything, and I still have that and I don't know whether you have that transcript or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that respect, did he say anything about the -- the Ustasha and Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: "We will route Ustashas and Chetniks and the people should not shed any tears because of us, the people, women, children, they mustn't shed any tears." Practically that's how I understood it. He was making a kind of warning that nothing should be done to those people, these elderly Croats that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now I'll take you to the 4th of September. Where were you on that date, which is the next day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: In the morning on the 4th of September, we all assembled in front of Safet Cibo's house, the president of the War Presidency of Jablanica, Konjic, and the free part of Prozor. We were outside in front of his house. I don't know who came, in which order. I think Sefer came last. I came before he did. Karic was there, and then when Sefer came, Karic said to him, "Sefer, there is a telegram for you from Arif Pasalic in which -- which says that the Ustashas" - and I understood it that it said that they would be attacking in two or three days, but in the order it's specifically stated - and I found that out later - they would attack the power plants. Sefer said, "Well, we will forestall them." I think that Karic or somebody said that, "The units from Jablanica are arriving." That's the first time I heard from him -- or actually, from Sarajevo -- Sarajevo -- and from Zenica -- Zenica, some artillery and so on and so forth. And then they were planning maybe they could attack on Wednesday or Thursday but we will then attack them actually on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any talk about the Sarajevo units?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, although, I didn't know which units these were. They just said that some units were supposed to come from Sarajevo. In the book, I mention it because later I got a document - I put that in later - what the requests were, which groups should come out of Sarajevo. I mentioned that there. What I knew at the time and what I published in the book is a little different, so I didn't want any misunderstandings to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will now show you a document, Mr. Hodzic. And this one is MFI161. It will come on your screen. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I received this document from the archives when I was working on my book and after the publication of the series of articles. At the time, I had no idea that it existed. But I did include it in the book because I -- I got it and so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this -- what is this and what does it say? In brief, if you can summarise.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It's for the command, command of the 1st Corps, for the commander. Then after the introduction about the difficult situation in Mostar, "I order, the Chief of Staff." "Deputy commander" is signed at bottom. "The Delta Brigade, parts of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade," and "Solakovic," this is mistake here. "All units over 200 fighters strong with complete equipment and weapons to be prepared and on Friday evening at the latest," and then so on and so forth. "To send to Bradina." So this is Sefer Halilovic's order to Vahid Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Corps to send the units, Delta, parts of 9th and 10th Brigade, and Solakovic's unit. That's it in brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you look at point number 2, what does Sefer Halilovic say there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: "If you believe that this would jeopardise the defence of Sarajevo, I will bear full personal responsibility."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- this -- you see this is on the 2nd of September, this -- this particular order. Was there any conversation about this?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd of September, 1993. Yes. Well, I didn't know that. I had no idea about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Sefer and the others converse about this, about the -- what you see, the contents of this document? Were they talking about the troops?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the troops arrived in Sarajevo at that time, on the 2nd of September. The Sarajevo troops? Had they arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody arriving, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it of any concern to Sefer that you heard about, that the Sarajevo troops had not arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- well, does that -- is that mentioned in my book? It probably is. When I was preparing the book and then with this document, it all fitted in with everything, because we returned to Sarajevo, so probably in order to incorporate it and link it up, it was probably -- perhaps I wrote that -- I don't know. Maybe he was concerned and maybe he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then set off for Deretvica [phoen] village after that, on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Neretvica. That's where the command of the 45th Mountain Brigade was. So we went off -- we set off from Cibo [as interpreted] towards Neretvica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone on the way?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the way from Jablanica to Konjic, we met Rasim Delic, Sulejman Vranj and Alija Loncevic, who were in a jeep. We were going from -- coming one direction. They were coming from the opposite direction. We stopped. In our car there was Sefer Halilovic, Cibo, Sefer's escort, and myself. And then Vehbija Karic and Zicro and Bilajac turned up from somewhere. I don't know how they turned up to be there. But anyway, we all met up and all went out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened at the car? Was there a conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it came to a conversation. Sefer said to Delic that Pasalic sent him a telegram saying that an HVO offensive against Mostar was being planned, the hydroelectric, that part of the area. And Delic told him that he had information about a Serb offensive at Igman and further in that direction being prepared as well. And one of them -- it's all in the book. I've forgotten. But anyway, it was about them coordinating these offences at the same time, and it was the first time I was actually afraid during the war that perhaps Bosnia could fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then you parted ways. You went your own ways.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went up in the direction of Neretvica. As far as I could tell, Mr. Halilovic was supposed to meet Salko Gusic, the commander of the 6th Corps, and the commander of the Muderis Brigade. And then we continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got back into the car after meeting Delic, did Sefer Halilovic say anything in -- in relation to meeting Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he turned to Dr. Cibo and myself -- or rather, he said to Cibo, "Cibo, tell Delic that I don't need him here. I am preparing for the offensive and I don't need him interfering with things here. That's what he said."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And apparently the witness says, "No interpreter is capable of translating this term."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then it is going to be my responsibility if the operation fails. And then he said -- and it was a bit weird to me, "Delic has been entrusted with the task of taking away as many powers from me as possible and so that I would only be left with a little bit of management, some -- something really minor. And I thought it was a bit strange that that should be the state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there you went -- and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went to Neretvica. Salko Gusic and Muderis were not there, and then we went back. We found the commander of the 45th Brigade, Haso Hakalovic, and we stayed there a little while and then we went back. Yes, whilst we were there, there was an agreement that there would be a meeting at Zuka's base at Donja Jablanica at 12.00, and so we went back down to Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would -- would point out in the transcript - excuse me, Mr. Hodzic - where the interpreter says "no interpreter is capable of interpreting this term." Could we have a confirmation as to why is that, Your Honours? Just I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could I ask the interpreter to tell us why --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. That's what the witness said, that apparently no interpreter is capable of interpreting this term.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But we feel we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm using Bosnian dialect. And when my book was being translated into English and apparently the terminology is different and the translator of my book also translated this sentence, and now it appears like different -- it appears to be different in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I think I'll leave that there, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic, for that clarification. And was there a meeting when you went back to Zuka's base?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we went to there, he was sitting in the entrance hall. General Delic -- no, he wasn't a general. Nobody was a general at that stage. So there was Delic there and Karic and the entire group, except for Sefer Halilovic. And then Sefer came and they went into the meeting room, and I stayed back with the lower-ranking commanders, and they were in the meeting but I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out later what the purport of that meeting was?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the meeting was about. All I know is that when we came out, it was agreed that Delic would go to Central Bosnia, and I don't know that he would be responsible for that area. And we went to Konjic -- oh, yeah, they agreed that everybody would go to Konjic, both Delic and this group and Sefer Halilovic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'll take you to 5th September. Where did you go on the 5th of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went to Konjic and we spent the night together at the ARK, Delic and Sefer. And then Delic went where he went. And we went in the direction of Dobro Polje, where there was a unit -- the Prozor Battalion was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did you -- yes, then where else did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Nowhere. We were there, up there, in Dobro Polje. Because we went through Neretvica and we went up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any talk about the units of the 9th and 10th Brigade at that -- on that -- at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. I still had no idea that they would be coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you this document, Mr. Hodzic. And its 65 ter number is 44, and it's 02122411. It will come up on your screen in a minute. Now, what is this document, Mr. Hodzic? Would you please be so kind as to tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, the command of the 1st Corps from Sarajevo is sending this to the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic, a reply about problems concerning the departure of these units from Sarajevo, that Caco and Celo -- well, this is to sum it up, because of rain and asking for their departure to be delayed by 24 hours. And then everything got much more complicated. And so finally those units never went out. That's it in a nutshell. And it is signed by Karavelic Vahid, who was the 1st Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this, you said, was a response to the first document I showed you.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose. It would the logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the time, you didn't know about these troops. You didn't have any conversation with Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, no, I had no idea. I had no idea of the order or the report or this communication. But let me tell you once again: I published the book in 1999, and it would be a bit ridiculous for me to say that I knew nothing at all. But I mean, I put it together on the basis of my own memories and the actual events and I incorporated this document, so it turns out, if you read the book, that I had prior knowledge of it, but I didn't. I mean, I spent -- I've wrote this book five or six years later, so I incorporated into the book certain events which I felt could be put in -- into certain paragraphs and then when I referred to a certain day, I thought it would be a good idea to refer to these documents, indicating to what was happening in the field. But at the time, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be MFI1290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in my respectful submission --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, it won't be any MFI at this stage, because the witness has simply said he never -- he never did see it at that time and had nothing to do with it. Frankly, Your Honours, as I understand it, Vehbija Karic -- sorry, pardon me. Vahid Karavelic is coming to give evidence in this case. And that is exactly the witness to put this document through. I have no objection to the questions about what this witness knew. They're perfectly appropriate questions, and the witness has answered them. Frankly, I can say that I won't be objecting to this document in the future when it comes through the appropriate witness. So although it's not really an appropriate time to give it an MFI number, if the Prosecutor insists on doing it, frankly because we know that Mr. Karavelic is coming, I won't object to it being marked, as I think about these things. So long as I have an undertaking that Mr. Karavelic is actually coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the purpose for giving it a number just for the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as I said before, at a later stage the Prosecution might formally tender this document into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So maybe that will be the proper time for us to discuss about the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honours I understand that. And I really just want an assurance from the Prosecutor that Mr. Karavelic is going to be called. And if that's the case, I won't object to this document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, are you in the position to shed some light?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Karavelic is on our list of witnesses and he certainly will be coming. And in any event, as Your Honour has said, that this is marked for identification and it's 290 - I correct myself - and I'm glad learned counsel actually decided to go back on his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, not only that. I could remind the Prosecutor to give an MFI number to the previous one that she forgot to do. It might be best if both of the orders are given an MFI number. I don't think the first one got one, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I believe it did. Your Honour, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe -- yeah, maybe --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous one has already been marked for identification as MFI161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you go back to Sarajevo on the 5th of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had -- had a meeting. I didn't know. I was outside. I was talk to the fighters. And then I found out that all of a sudden that evening we would be leaving for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the time why you went back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. And it looks in the book as if I knew, because, of course, I was quoting the documents. But I mean, I was simply saying for what reason Sefer was going, but I avoided saying whether I knew or did not know. I was just telling the story, giving an account of these events. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now I will take you back -- I will take you forward to 7th September. Now, on that particular date, did you go back to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of September, I went back to the Chief of Staff, Mr. Halilovic, at 7.00 in the evening and I met Celo in the corridor and I said, "So are you going as well, Celo?" And he said "Yes." And that's when I found out that those units were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was there when -- when you -- when you went to the 1st Corps forward command post?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, we went through the tunnel and we came again to the forward command post of the 1st Corps in Hrasnica, and we found Celo there, Adnan Solakovic, Pezo, and I think Cibo was with us as well. I'm not sure. But certainly Cibo was there. I think he was in the car with us or -- but he had his own car, so I don't know. And then there was a brigade, the Hrasnicka Brigade [as interpreted], commander -- my brain has just stopped. I can't remember. Oh, yeah, Fikret Pravljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was Caco there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Caco wasn't there. And then they told Sefer that Caco didn't want to go to Herzegovina, that he didn't want to lead his unit to Herzegovina. And Sefer asked, "Well, what's all that about?" And then he was told that he had had a disagreement with Fikret Pravljak and others because apparently Caco's fighters, there were still consequences from that Igman operation and apparently they were stealing sheep from the people and Fikret and his people were interfering with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was Sefer Halilovic's view on the matter, about Caco not coming along?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He -- well, I don't know what his attitude was, but -- actually, I wasn't sure that he would be able to convince Caco to get going, and he asked Celo to accompany him and tried to convince him. And then Celo said, "No, no, no, you don't know, Sefer. You don't know Caco. If one of his men dies, I'm going to be blamed for it and I'm going to have problems."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to be quite clear about this, Mr. Hodzic, you said Sefer wanted to persuade Caco; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He wanted to invite Caco with Celo's help to take his unit down there. I don't know whether Caco himself, but that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then what did Sefer do?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: They went and they came back quickly and they said yes, that Caco's unit and Caco himself as well were going to go. I didn't know that Caco was going to go. Perhaps the unit. But the crunch was that yes, they were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when they set off, where did they set off to? To find Caco? When you said "they went and they came back," what was the purpose of them going and what where did they go?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the purpose was to go look for Caco and convince him to send his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did Caco come to this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He did not come with them but at a certain point somebody said, "Okay. There's Caco in the corridor, but he doesn't want to come in." And then Adnan Solakovic went to the door and he said, "Well, Caco, why aren't you coming in?" And then he said "No." And after a while he did come in and that was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when he came in?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He came in, and he was rather sceptical and distrustful of myself and Cibo in particular. He was looking at us sideways and he had a problem his -- with his hand because he had been wounded and so his fingers had been cut off, so he was hiding his hand under the table. But then all of a sudden he thought a little bit and then he started talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, the main thing was the characteristic aspect that we knew about with regard to Caco was that he was going to Kopljari and then there was somebody who was called Robin Hood and the entire conversation was focussed on that, but it was all a joke, about how they went digging. And I think -- it was about the media. Perhaps even the world media. When it came to Vedran Smajlic, he used to play violoncello and he took this artist to go digging, and many people took an interest and nobody was able to do anything. May I just add something else? And a couple of months earlier there was the first anniversary of the massacre at the Vasemiskina Ulica and there was an incredible image when this cello player at the place where a shell killed and wounded many people, and he was playing there, and I think it was broadcast by the world media. And this person on that day was supposed to go back and play there again. And my paper by coincidence, by coincidence sent me to report on that event, and I went there, and everybody was expecting Caco to give in. And he did not give in. He didn't let him come. And in my text I did mention something -- I can't remember, but I said something along the lines of an anniversary -- no, the heading was a bit nicer, but I said something "An anniversary without Vedran and without his cello." And when I went back to the newspaper and I gave an account of what happened and I wrote my article and everybody said, "Well, how is it possible that nobody can do anything about this Caco person?" And I -- and then they said, "Why can't Alija? Why can't Sefer?" And then somebody at the paper said the following: "Now they can't, neither one nor the other, because Caco sent a message to all -- whoever Alija intervenes for or on whoever's behalf Alija intervenes will get 30 days more and if Sefer intervenes on their behalf, they'll be hanged." And so we went back to Hrasnica, we talked about it. We laughed at him. He spoke at great length. And so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be entirely clear on the matter, you are talking about Vedran Smajlic being taken to dig trenches. Is that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Caco is the one who took him?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, he said yes. Yes, he said yes. I was called as well and Sefer called, and apparently he said he liked it. But Caco said, "Everybody keeps calling me and saying that he is an artist and I am an artist," and because he used to play an accordion and he was on the TV orchestra. And then he said, "I am an artist as well, but we need to defend Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the conversation which was occurring at that time with Caco?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but it was a kind of joke, all of it. That was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Sefer say anything about Vedran Smajlic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, he said to Vedran, but by way of joke, he said, "I was asked to call you but then I said maybe he likes it up there," but it was a joke, once again. And there was about -- "Is this okay? Perhaps he is going out to cheat on his wife and then the wife calls me and she says, "Is my husband with you?" And I said, "Yes, yes, he's here with me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sefer say anything else about -- that whether he had tried to intervene with Caco, on this matter?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Sefer -- well, no, Adnan, Pezo, and Celo were the ones who talked to Caco and induced him to tell stories and then he would get all fired up about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what happened later on that day? And we're still on 7th September, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: When we set out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just intervene there? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The witness hasn't said that this conversation took place on the 7th of September. He said that he set off with Halilovic on the 7th of September in the evening. And it just ought to be made clear whether at this stage we've moved into the early morning of the 8th of September or whether it remains on the 7th of September. That should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that should be clarified, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've taken the witness chronologically through his evidence, but I will certainly clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, can you tell us when was this? What date and time this conversation with Caco and people took place.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, we set out at 8.00, perhaps a little built later. And then we went through the tunnel. It took a while to get through the tunnel. And then we went to the IKM. And then it all took several hours. So it was still the 7th when we were at IKM, the 7th of September when we were there in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time was it when Caco was found and this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. It could have been 9.00 or 10.00 approximately. I'm not at all sure. At any rate, at night, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps even at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything which concerned Sefer at the time about the Sarajevo fighters at that time, straight after that -- this?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, the main problem was that the fighters had to be taken to Jablanica and that local commander, the local brigade commander who had cars and lorries and drivers, Fikret Prevljak, wouldn't allow the lorries to take them there. And then the Chief of Staff could not actually issue an order to this brigade commander to take the fighters to Jablanica, and he didn't allow it and he didn't allow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, I would like to ask you: Did you and Sefer have a conversation about Caco afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean when we left, when it was agreed that Cibo would try and find some means of transport? Well, when we set out, I said, "Sefer, well, this is the first time I see this Caco person, but I don't think he's all there." And he said, "No, he isn't." And he said, "Well, I really don't think he is -- well, I couldn't quite say he was a lunatic. I can't remember what sort of word I used then, but I said that there was something wrong with him. And then he said, "Okay. He is a part of the realities of war and he is useful." But he did have good fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he said "is part of the reality of this war but he's useful." What was he referring to? Useful in what way?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: "Yes, but useful." Of course when we talk about Caco, we think also in terms of his unit. He is one thing and his units are something else. His units were guarding the most dangerous part in the area of Trebevic and they managed to defend that area from the Serbs several times. And in 1995 -- well, that was fate. His trenches were there and there was a horrible Serb offensive in that area and he had established, created those trenches and even though it was done in a slightly illegal way, well, they managed to defend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we are into -- into the night of 7th September. Where did you go that night?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We went to Jablanica. It was already light. Around 7.00 we came to Donja Jablanica in the same way. I came out of the car, because I was supposed to stay there, while Sefer went back to Zuka's apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see? Did you see Celo's soldiers on that day in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I tried to get some sleep. I got up at about 10.00 or 10.30. I don't know. And then I saw Bilajac, Karic, and Zicro Suljevic in front of the command, and two of my colleagues from the university, former inmates. They were freed. They will later figure in my story about all of this. Kasim Korijenic, and Serif Krgo. They were playing chess. I spoke with Karic a little bit. Sefer wasn't there. Karic's son was there also. I had developed some pictures at the newsroom, and I gave the photos to Karic's son to give to Zuka and the other soldiers. And then I asked, "Cica, when will this offensive of ours begin?" And he said, "Well, maybe tomorrow." Karic said, "Yes, yes, it's possible." So I just played chess with my colleagues for a little bit, and I don't know where they went and how they went. I don't know that about Karic. Zicro, Bilajac. They left. I stayed to play chess, chess, chess. And then later I was sitting in front of the base. Every day expelled people would be passing by from Herzegovina, Bosniaks. They would be passing by the base carrying their belongings. Then you would see two elderly people, something a little different. They were going in the opposite direction, towards Capljina. The woman was obviously disturbed. She was in her slippers. And she said, "I have to look after my daughter's children in Capljina," but it was about 100 kilometres to Capljina. There were no more Bosniaks in Capljina any more. They had been expelled. She said, "I'm going to look after my daughter's children while she's at work." And then we were trying to convince her not to do that. Later I found out that they had gotten killed on the road. They were on their way to Mostar. This happened on the way to Mostar. Just by accident I found out that they had been killed. I found out later from Kasim Korijenic that a new group of inmates had come from Dretelj. He said they looked like they had come from Auschwitz. And I thought that I would speak with them a little bit. But I was sleepy and this chess had sort of pulled me in a different direction so that day I didn't go and then that morning -- yes, well, I won't go on any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now, the question originally had been: Did you see the soldiers, the Sarajevo soldiers, pass by that morning, on the 8th September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. Yes, I saw them I think some of them even stopped and I think I even made a photo of them when they stopped in front to have base. Maybe this happened around 11.00 and some of them were passing and they were waving to us and then they passed by ask they left. I think some of them stayed briefly, but I'm not sure. It seems to me I, but I'm not sure, but this is already a little bit beyond what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Halilovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I did not have any communications with Sefer Halilovic from the time he left me there until the next day. But I could be mistaken, but I think that sometime I -- very well. I did or didn't. But I don't know. I think that I did at some point see him when I was playing chess for a very brief period. But I cannot be sure about it. But mostly it's true that I didn't have any communication with him from that morning until the next evening when we met again at the base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I think you were asked to slow down, Mr. Hodzic. And you've been -- been very good and you have been slow, but just to remind you again. How far was -- when you thought you saw Sefer Halilovic on the 8th, how far away was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be a speculative question eliciting a speculative answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think so. Because the witness was not sure whether he saw Mr. Halilovic or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the witness said he -- he thought he -- he saw Mr. Halilovic. I would like to clarify, if I may, where -- where was it that he thought he saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could make sure whether this witness saw Mr. Halilovic on that day. Then you could ask the second question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Sefer Halilovic on that day, which is the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I have an image, as I was playing chess, that I perhaps just glanced at him briefly. It appeared as if he was there and I continued to play chess and that's the whole story. I don't know if I did or didn't. I have the impression that I did, but I cannot state that definitely. He was definitely not there when Zicro, Bilajac, these three were there. That's for sure, Bilajac and Karic. Because I don't know whether they were waiting for him or not, but mostly I -- I don't know. He did not appear there. He would have appeared in my book had I seen him, because Bilajac, Zicro, and Karic do appear but his function is not there that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Now I'm into 9th September. What did you do on 9th September?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: With my colleague Kasim Korijenic I went to Jablanica, where the inmates were accommodated, a new batch of inmates who had been freed from Dretelj. They were placed at the school, and we went to the school. He told me that this Gacanin is in that group and there was a lot of talk about him when the first group of inmates came, and they had tried to cut his throat at the camp in Dretelj. So he came with the first group of refugees. We went to the school, where there were about maybe 350 inmates. And it was very difficult to me to bear it. I couldn't write down anything. I just asked several of them to come outside. There was such a terrible stench there. I described it as the smell of dead bodies. When you go inside, you can smell this smell after an hour or two. And then these people, I guess after 75 days their skill was beginning to die off and that smell was the smell of death, 100 per cent, the same smell you smell when you enter a morgue. I couldn't stand it. And then I asked a few of them, I said, "Please come out. My blitz is not working. Will you please come out so I can take pictures of you." Some of them came out, seven or eight men, and I took photos of them. They looked as if they were from Auschwitz. You have a picture of that in my book. They said, "Well, I'm just looking at them." They said, "There are people who are in a worse state than we are." I said, "Where are they?" They said, "They're in the hospital. And I went to the house and I found out a few of those who had been brought in and I had an interview with them and then it happened that there were some captured HVO soldiers there and then I spoke with them. I spoke with the Bosniak inmates and with these HVO fighters, who had been wounded and who were receiving medical treatment there. So there you go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Jablanica and meet some acquaintances from MUP?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I finished the interview at 5.00 in the afternoon. When I finished, I looked at my watch and I will never forget that. This -- two days before that, they said, "Delic, Sefer, here they are coming. Those people over there, Serbs from this side," I'm looking at these inmates, these people, and at that time I was really -- my biorhythm was below zero. Without any hope that Bosnia can be saved. And then when I went down there to Jablanica, I met a younger man. He was not too far from my neighbourhood, but I didn't know his name. I Knew him from seeing him around. And then he said -- oh, yes, I know his name. His name is Nedzad Surkovic. And then he said, "Did you hear what happened in Grabovica? I said, "No, I didn't." He said somebody killed a five-member Croat family. Immediately the first thing that came to mind after what I had seen in Kostajnica when I was there and when those people were threatening those elderly people is that some of those expellees or inmates had done the killing. I knew that I couldn't go there, but I wanted to go there, if I could at least film it or -- or take pictures clandestinely, and this was in front of the MUP. We went into the MUP, and I asked, "Is it possible to go there? How?" And they said, "No, no, no way. It's all closed," so I didn't really insist on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did -- why did they say that, "It's all closed"? Why did they say that it was closed?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: They said that you couldn't pass through. That's what Nedzad and these others said. They said, "You can't go through. You can't pass."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you any reason as to why you couldn't pass through to Grabovica village?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I think that you couldn't pass, that it was closed, in the sense that, you know, the army was there. In that sense. I don't know. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long I was in Jablanica, for a little while. But anyway, I asked this Necko [phoen] to drive me. He had a car at his disposal, to take me to Donja Jablanica, where I was staying. I didn't have the will to do anything, to write anything, nothing about the inmates, the dead, the hospital. I didn't really want to do anything, and I went to Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were at Donja Jablanica, did Sefer Halilovic come along?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I sat down. I can't say now how long I was sitting. I sat down in this sort of waiting room or this entrance hall. That's where people had their meals, and that's where Delic and Sefer had their meeting earlier. So I was sitting in front of that building where fighters were sitting. Anybody could sit there. There were benches there. You could drink coffee there. And I was sitting alone at the table and that's when Sefer came from up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when Sefer came? And can you also indicate the time when Sefer came, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No, I really couldn't. It's very flexible. It could be 8.00, 9.00, it could be 7.00, it could be 6.00 -- well, it couldn't be 6.00. It was after 6.00 for sure. So I really couldn't fix the time. He sat next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was silent, and I asked him, "Where were you?" And he said, "I was in Neretvica, towards Konjic," somewhere, anyway, in that area, and that he was with Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, who was the minister for energy. That's what he said. And then -- and the fighters were already sitting around there. As soon as Sefer would come, the soldiers would start gathering around him. So I kind of whispered to him, "What happened in Grabovica down there?" And he said, "Yes." And I said, "Well, what do you think that that -- about whether any of these inmates or the refugees killed this family?" And he said, "Well, that's what I think too." The fighters were around, as I was saying. They were saying, "Hey, Sefer. How are you? What's going on?" And that's when we interrupted our conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you whispered to him, "What happened in Grabovica down there," he simply said "yes." What did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I assumed that he knew about the crime. I in the beginning thought that this was just this family of five that was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you how you had heard and what you knew about these crimes or -- sorry, the killings in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't, because there were a lot of fighters around us asking, "Sefer" -- and so it was impossible to communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these fighters asking Sefer?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember them asking anything that related to the crime. No, I don't remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Sefer's demeanour at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, he was quiet. You could simply see -- well, perhaps if I hadn't asked him anything, he wouldn't have said two words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else, whether he was going to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: As I said, we didn't continue our conversation about that. Perhaps as many as 20 fighters had assembled around us and people were asking him different things. The fighters actually took the talk into quite a different area from what Sefer and I were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you sitting there and when did Sefer then leave?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how long. He went in the direction of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sefer? Is that -- are you referring --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not quite sure. Yes, yes, Sefer. I think -- I think he did. I don't know. I think he did go towards Jablanica, but I wasn't really paying much attention to that, but I think he did go to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't tell you where he was going.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me, but it seems to me that he did go to Jablanica, but I'm not quite sure about that, but I -- I think so. It seemed like that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and presumably you went to bed.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Probably I did, or I played chess. I don't know what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the next day, which is the 10th of September. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we could take a break, you know, before we go to the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, before the break, we had started on the 10th of September. Can you tell us where you were on that day, please.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I was planning to go to Jablanica in the morning. The base was in Donja Jablanica, so it's about 7 or 8 kilometres away from Jablanica. And I was waiting for some kind of transportation in front of the base in order to get to Jablanica, but no car came by and nobody was there who could take me there, Zuka or anyone, if I had asked them to. So I was sitting in front of the base and Celo came by in a car and he stopped the car in front of the base. He came out of the car and passed by, and I asked him, "Celo, are you going to Jablanica?" "Yes." I looked in the back, there were two boys sitting. There was enough space next to the boys and I was waiting for Celo to come back quickly. At the bar in the base, Nihad Bojadzic was standing. He's Zuka's deputy. And the two of them were talking. I looked to see if Celo was going, but they kept talking. I didn't hear anything of what they were saying. After a while, Celo came out, opened the car door, and asked the boys to come out. The boys came out, and he brought them into Zuka's command and handed them over to Nihad Bojadzic, and then he came back and went into the car, and I thought these were perhaps children of those people who had been expelled. Maybe they were tired or something. I thought those were the kids. So I got to Jablanica with Celo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see Emin Zebic there when you went to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the MUP building right away. Actually, the public security station, where this Zebic was chief. And they gave me a typewriter for my use. They were the only ones in Jablanica that had a working typewriter, and they gave me paper. So I started to work. We had coffee. Cicko was there and quite a few other people, and that's when I found out that the crime in Grabovica was committed by some fighters from Sarajevo and it looked like they were Celo's soldiers and it wasn't just the family of five that was killed but perhaps some 15 to 20 people were killed. They were talking about an engineer. Everybody was a little bit down. They mentioned this younger engineer who was working in the army production or manufacturing facility, and perhaps they killed him too. And that's when I thought that -- well, they said that only two boys were saved. So then I put two and two together and thought perhaps it was the two boys that Celo had brought to the base in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask them any questions, whether they had been to Grabovica or not?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I asked them something to the effect, "Were you there?" And they said, "You couldn't go." They tried but they didn't manage, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say why they could not manage to get into the village?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was -- wasn't -- that there was a checkpoint, if you wanted to get in, something like that. That the checkpoint was set up by the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you meet Bakir Alispahic on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon, late. I spent quite some time in Jablanica. There is one street in Jablanica, and I was just passing by MUP and then Bakir came out and his escort and Zebic, and I just spoke with him briefly. It was raining and it was still raining. And by the time he reached the car, we talked a little bit about the crime. And he told me then. I understood that and I spoke to Karic about it, that he -- he mentioned Sefer and Karic, but I understood that -- it to be about how this commission will be formed, headed by Karic. And later I asked Karic, "Did you do anything?" And he said, "This is the first time I'm hearing about this commission." But I remember it. I think he even mentioned the public prosecutor or something like that. But this was just as we were walking. He told me he was going to the ARK for a meeting in Konjic, where Sefer and Cibo will also -- will be -- and Mahmutcehajic, and that's what he said -- he went. And then he went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you returned to Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: After that, I don't know how. At that time moment, Zuka came by in the jeep with Edib Sahic inside. Zuka was quite affected because they, I think, killed one of his men. He was very angry. He said, "This is a slap in the face to everyone. They will think that it was my men who did it. These guys should be arrested. They should be hanged," something like that. Saric also said, "Yes, this is a slap in the face to our army." And then I asked him, "And what about these boys?" Because I had already put two and two together. He said, "Well, they're in a safe place. They're with me and they're safe. I will protect them." And he said that he was protecting those people there the entire time, the civilians and, "Look at what these people did now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- did he say -- what did you understand -- who was it that Zuka was blaming? Who were "these people"?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The killers, the ones who did the killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But when you said "my soldiers may be blamed," that's Zuka's soldiers, who was he putting the blame on, Zuka himself?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember. That perhaps somebody could make a false accusation. Perhaps don't know. I mean it's his soldiers that are there. That his soldiers committed it, and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But -- but you never got from him who he thought had done it.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No. Later we talked, but it was immediately known about Celo -- well, actually, there was talk about it. It wasn't known. I mean, I returned to Sarajevo, but I wasn't quite sure who did what for years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to 11 September. Did you meet somebody from the Igmanski Vukovi who came to Donja Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was sitting again. As I say, I was sitting alone in Zuka's base. In this room. There was no electricity. There was just a candle. And a man came up to me. I didn't know him. He sat down next to me. I said, "Who are you?" He said, "Well, you were making an interview down there with me when you came the first day. I'm from the Igman Wolves." And that's when I understood that that was the person who was the most important next to Saric. I knew Saric. But when I was there, he wasn't there. So he told me what he knew about how the crime happened. I asked him, "Did you see it?" He said, "Yes, I saw it all, friend. I can't sleep. I can't eat. These were wonderful people. They gave us everything we asked for. Two days ago I was in that family." He probably meant the Zadro family that was killed. "They made a pie for us." I said, "Did they line them up and shoot them?" He said, "No, they went from house to house killing." And I said, "What did they do with the bodies?" He said, "They threw them into the Neretva." "Could you help them in any way," I said. He said, "No, these people were under the influence of drugs, alcohol." He said, "They attacked even four or five Bosniaks -- Bosniak women, refugees, Muslims. They tried to rape some of them. Some tried to escape to our base but then they fired at us and we returned the fire," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'll take you to 12th September, Mr. Hodzic, and I would ask you: Did you interview these two children on that date?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the 12th in the morning, Kasim Korijenic, this colleague of mine -- actually, the day before he said that they slept at their place, that Zuka had designated this soldier, a tall guy, Sjenicak to be with these boys. And he was in the same room where this Kasim Korijenic was and he had a masters degree and this other man was a poet. He had put them in the room with the best people to sleep in that room. And then in the morning, when this Sjenicak came back from breakfast. He was taking them to the base. He said, "Well, here the boys are," and that's when I went sort of in between the buildings because I couldn't really do it in the open -- open and that's when we sat down and I spoke with them. Well, we at didn't actually speak together. They just told me the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, very, very briefly, Mr. Hodzic, please, would you tell us what the children told you.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The boys told me -- I put down all the names, Goran and Zoran Zadro. One was 11. The other one was 13. They said on that day, on the 9th, i the morning at 11.00 three soldiers came in front of their house. They had quite specific haircuts, shaved -- the back of the heads were shaved and they were easily recognisable. And I asked them what ethnicity they were. And they said they were Croats. And then they asked whether they had any livestock and they said, "Yes, we did." And then their grandfather and grandmother and father went to the barn to show them the cattle and that's when they heard the shots and they concluded that they had been killed. Then their mother gave them a sign that they should run to the forest. They escaped to the forest. They saw from the woods how their mother and their sister were being taken out. It was a little girl. They were hungry and they probably weren't dressed properly either. So before evening they came back near the road. And that's when I think they said three soldiers came by and asked them to surrender, to -- not to surrender but to come up to them without being afraid. And they took them back to the base or wherever they were. They gave them something to eat. And then they took them home so that they could take some clothes, so that they could dress. And they came in front of the house and they saw -- said that there were three dead bodies near the barn. That was probably the grandfather, the grandmother, and the father. And in front of the house, their mother was lying down and her daughter - their sister - covered with a sheet, and then they said how -- I'm sorry, can I -- can I -- wait. Can I pause for a bit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Hodzic. Please take your time, Mr. Hodzic. There's no hurry.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: They said they had uncovered the mother. She had been shot in the chest, and they saw their little sister, who was three and a half years old, who had been shot in the face. And then he said one thing, a sentence that has been haunting me for years. He said, "That girl, three and a half years old," he said "was blond and had green eyes." That was like an arrow going through my heart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Hodzic, did these children tell you anything about the way they had been treated since they were discovered by the -- the -- the Bosnian army, the people who had handled them? Did they make any comments about their treatment?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything else. I took note of their names and the little one said something else as well, that he had everything like he was the most -- as if he had been the owner of the house "I had a house and the livestock and now I have nothing left and where are my goats now," and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sefer Halilovic come to the base in Donja Jablanica when the children were there?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: The children left. They left with this other guy. I don't know where they went to. And I stayed with Kasim and -- I mean, I did meet them, but then they left, supposedly to that house. I don't know where he took them. And then after a while I -- somebody else came, and then Mr. Halilovic came and Cibo with him. And I think we had spoken on the phone in the evening and we had agreed that -- I think they had come to pick me up or something. Maybe they had some other business to attend to. Well, I can't really remember. But at any rate, we went in the direction of Dobro Polje and the Prozor Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell -- did you tell Mr. Halilovic about the conversation you'd had with the children?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I just didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're still on the 12th, Mr. Hodzic, and you're going off to Prozor. What was the purpose of now you going off to Prozor with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, to prepare for battle, for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with you as you were going towards Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Cibo, Dr. Cibo, and his entourage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the way there, did you discuss this massacre in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Sefer what had happened in relation to that meeting at the ARK, at Konjic, where they meet -- where they had that meeting a couple of days earlier, and I think Sefer started saying -- or maybe Cibo. I can't remember precisely. But they said that they did talk and that they talked about the massacre and Bakir Alispahic asked for the operation to be interrupted and Cibo said -- and Cibo butted in and said -- and at that stage I asked him, "Are you mad? Don't talk about interrupting operations. What we need to do is save 100.000 people, 100.000 Bosniaks from Herzegovina," and then Sefer tried to calm things down and he said, "Let's make it clear. I don't approve of what has happened down there, but there is a certain sequence of events and doing things. We first have to complete the offensive and, you know, carry out the punishment, and then there are people who are in charge of that, to investigate crimes, and then the legal procedure would follow." And it was totally in line with Sefer's views in other situations earlier. He said, "Okay. This person is in charge of legal matters and this is an army," et cetera. And it was the same thing when there was a disagreement between Zuka and Hakalovic and then they -- on the 2nd of September, there was some sort of ambush or something to kill someone, and then he said, "You don't need to settle these accounts between the two of you. We have a certain legal procedure. There is a person in charge of that who is going to look into the matter, and everything has to be done according to the provisions of the law." And so that's how he said that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, I will show you another document, if I may, and this one is D157, Your Honours. It will come on your screen in a minute. Is it there before you, Mr. Hodzic? I can't see it -- yes. Can you tell us what this --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what this document is and whether you've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it before. So it's a letter. I can't see the signature, but I know what it is -- yeah, Rasim Delic, the commander from Visoko. He is writing -- Can you scroll it down a little bit? Yeah, the headquarters and the Supreme Command -- forward the command personally -- Jablanica, the command of the 6th Corps. So Delic is writing that he had found out from the Chief of Staff of the 6th Corps about the planned combat operations in the direction of Prozor and Mostar, and in this respect he orders to investigate the decision in terms of the feasibility and the possibility of carrying out the task and in line of the outcome of that investigation to change a decision and to bring it all down to the actual feasibility level and to look into the data about genocide of the civilian population on the part of the members of the 9th Brigade of the 1st Corps, and in case it is confirmed, to isolate the perpetrators, undertake all the necessary and strict measures, and to do everything in order to prevent that from happening again and to order the deputy commander of the 9th Brigade of the 1st Corps to go back to Sarajevo straight away about solving the problems in the unit and to -- and for him to be informed about all this straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when was the first time you actually saw this and who showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time in the morning of the 9th, when Sefer came to Jablanica. He said to me, "Okay. I have something to show you," and he showed it to me and he read it out to me. And I didn't have my glasses, so I couldn't read it myself. And so he read through the first part of the letter from Delic to him, and then he read through this point, that is to say, to scale down the scope of the operations, and he said that it wouldn't be done, that they would not scale the operation down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the transcript says that you first saw it in the morning of the 9th. But would you look at the date of this document, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I did not say the 9th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then the --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the 12th. Maybe I made a mistake. I'm sorry. I do apologise. On the 12th. So on that morning, not the 12th but -- not the 9th. On the 12th. On that morning that we set out to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was on the way, wasn't it, as you were going to Prozor that this document was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no, actually, before the departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that Sefer said you're not going to -- that the operations were not going to be scaled down. Did he say anything about the other leg of it? Is --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: That there was no need to scale it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say about -- regarding the genocide committed against the civilian population by members of the 1st Corps 9th Motorised Brigade and to isolate the perpetrators and take the energetic measures? Did he have anything to say about that aspect of Rasim Delic's order?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. He did not read out that part to me, nor did he say anything in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else about continuing with the offensive?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's somewhere in the book, but I really can't remember at this stage. He did say once that that offensive was going to make a contribution to the liberation of the country, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some later stage interview Rasim Delic about this particular 12th September order, later on?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you talk to him about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, would the witness just excuse me a moment, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, when the Prosecution has decided not to call Mr. Delic himself, this evidence just can't be led. I'm not talking the objection on the basis that it's hearsay, although it obviously is hearsay. But when the Prosecutor makes a decision not to call the witness for whatever reasons they have, to lead this material, in my submission, just can't help this Tribunal to make any decision. It couldn't assist you with anything. What Mr. Delic may have said about things at a later time -- currently you don't even have a time when that interview took place. I mean, we don't know when it was, and the Prosecutor hasn't asked yet.
