But -- well, perhaps I'll just say at this stage perhaps the -- we should find out, first of all, when this interview took place before I say any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I believe that the conversation conducted between the two persons, so we could hear one side of view concerning of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for how much weight the Bench should give to that piece of evidence, that's something -- we will discuss it and consider it at a much later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that Mr. Delic is not called by the Prosecution at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any possibility for the Defence to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we know where he is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But I'll -- I mean, I would say as a certainty, no. We could discuss this matter in another way. I'm -- the objection is not to the witness giving his account. I'm -- in a sense I'm not concerned by -- by Mr. Hodzic. He -- if the Court wishes to hear -- hear it, then -- then you'll make an order to that effect, of course. I just make the point at this stage that perhaps my objection was a little bit premature because we don't know when this interview took place and perhaps that should be asked before we go much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Well, Ms. Chana, maybe you should lay down some foundations about the time or maybe place -- the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, would you please tell Their Honours, when was it that you interviewed Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the date was exactly, but it was published in Oslobodjenje, that interview, so you can find out the date, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before you published your book or after? This is an attempt to -- to remind you of the date.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It must be before, because it's in the book. Perhaps it was around the time when the book was about to be published. I move asked him on that occasion and then he might have told me, "It is possible but maybe it's not the case." I asked both him and Sefer. And he said to me that Sefer did not send anything in relation to that report, and then I said to Sefer -- and not just about this report. But other things. And Delic said no and Sefer said yes, he kept him up to date on everything and on a regular basis, and so that's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, to go back again to try to pinpoint the date --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: And I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I said, to go back to try and pinpoint the date, when was your book published?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I hope you don't mind, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year, Mr. Hodzic? That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can I just assist here? I don't mind if the witness is shown the book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just in terms of that, it's not controversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The witness could be shown the book or even my friend could read it out to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, you could lead evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I do write a great deal, so I can't help forgetting things.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I show the witness -- it's not in B/C/S. It's 1992 -- no, it can't be. 1996. That's what it says on the book.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, it can't be.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It was the first thing -- no, that was the first book. Yeah, but the year 2000. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before then? How many months would you say would it be before?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: It must be before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long before you published -- the first -- the book was published? About, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I think the printing process took about six months, and so how much earlier than that -- it could be anything. If I knew you were asking to -- you were going to ask this question, I could, you know, check with Oslobodjenje and then I would be able to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But it would be fair to say it was sometime in 2000 that you had an interview with Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 1999. I don't know. I really can't say. But maybe it was -- sometime between 1999 and 2000, because the series of articles came out in January 1999 and so it was sometime in between. So either in 1999 or in 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us about this interview. What did you -- did you discuss with him? First I'll talk to you in relation to the 12th September order, this order that I've just shown you.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: With whom? With whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have to renew any objection mere. Your Honours, this is really an attempt of the Prosecutor in my submission to have the account of Mr. Delic put before the Tribunal at a time when the Prosecution has renounced to call that individual. Now, it's quite evident here -- well, no, I won't make a speech about it. What I submit is that you now know the date of this interview. You know that it happens in 2000. You know that -- you know a number of facts about what had already happened by the year 2000. And frankly, this is too late. It's just way late. It's just why -- it couldn't be probative of any matter before this Tribunal what was said, and the witness can give his evidence in good faith, of course. It's just a question that it's not going to help you what was said in a conversation by the year 2000. So I submit that this shouldn't be pursued now. It's too remote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, when we evaluate that piece of evidence, we'll take your objection into the consideration; but, however, this piece of the evidence could be presented in this courtroom. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, would you tell us: When you interviewed Mr. Delic, did you ask him about the 12th September 1993 order that we have just shown you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I did an interview with Delic after this book, a long interview, and it was the front-page article. Precisely when things were beginning to heat up about this Grabovica business and I asked him about Grabovica and all that. I mean, if you have any documentation, perhaps you could show it to me, because I really don't know. I have -- I simply can't seem to make the connection. What do you have in mind? The interview after, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many interviews did you have with Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- we're at 12th September 1993. I've shown you this order by Mr. Delic to Halilovic to reconsider the scope of the operation. Right?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to talk to Mr. Delic about this order?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've told you. All that boils down to the fact that Sefer didn't inform him, and then I asked Sefer, and he claimed he did. And at this stage, I mean there are perhaps two pages of the text, my questions and his answers, but I can't recollect a single word. I mean, it is all in writing. Even if I wanted to hide something, I wouldn't be able to, but I am able to forget things, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just to be clear, when you said that it "boils down to the fact that Sefer did inform him and I asked Sefer and he claimed he did." Now, can you tell us what he was talking about? Inform him? Inform him of what?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what to say. Perhaps the operation, at what stage they were doing what, and they had this Dzankovic person there who was in charge of security and it was certainly his task to keep reporting. It wasn't he himself personally had to take care of everything. There was a distribution of tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did publish this order in your book, did you not, Mr. Hodzic, this 12th September order?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did. I got it and I published it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I made a written request. It was all totally legal. And I made the request to the commander of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The request was approved, and I got it from the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I got his approval from -- for some other operations, and then a second commander and then a third commander, I got their approval to make use of the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to this controversy that you talked about earlier on when you interviewed Sefer and Halilovic -- sorry, and Delic about being informed. I'd ask you: Is it informed about events on the ground in Herzegovina at the time of combat? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was about fighting in Herzegovina, did he have any information. And he said that as to the outcome and the course of battle, that he had received no information. It seems to me that that is my impression, that he said that was the way it was and then Sefer said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to -- now, we are back to the 12th again, and you are on your way. And this Sefer is reading out this order to you. You said you -- you couldn't see -- you didn't have your glasses, so you couldn't read it yourself. But you saw Sefer reading from the document, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No. Point 1, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hodzic? "Point 1, yeah," can you please tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Well, to look into the decision in terms of scaling the operation down, and Sefer said that he wouldn't do it, that there would be no scaling-down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring to his attention any matter about the consequences of not scaling down the operation and listening to Mr. Delic's order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. That's, with respect, a relatively misleading question. If you have a look at -- at what the order itself requires, it requires Halilovic to consider the matter. There's no order there telling him to scale it down at all, and the witness shouldn't have that put to him in that form. The witness has seen the order before and has published it in his book, and it ought to be put to him properly and not in the form it was, so I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, I believe you have to -- to lead this witness step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And this time I -- I think learned counsel is quite correct in that objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I will ask you is: When -- when Sefer was asked to reconsider the scale of the operation, he had -- you said he obviously disagreed. Was there any other discussion about -- what the consequences of his disagreeing.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, not about the consequences. Quite the contrary. When we got there, we no longer spoke about that. But the same thing was recounted to me in almost the same terms by Vehbija Karic when we got there and found the team in question ask then Vehbija said, "Sefer, there is a telegram from Delic for you," and that's probably what he said in mind. And Sefer said, "Yes, I know." And then Karic said, "No, no, no, it's out of the question. We can't scale down the operation." And Sefer said, "We'll follow the original plan."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: And they used to operate as a team anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and when Karic said that, did he refer to the same order? The 12th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just sorry. No, I object --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, may I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before the witness is entitled to be asked that question - it's not the witness's fault - it has to be sure that the witness saw the order that Karic had. If it helps the Tribunal at a later time that my friend may choose to ask the question, "Did he infer that it was the same order?", which may -- may have some value. I doubt it, but it might. But it has to be established that he saw that order before that question can be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I had done that, that -- was Karic talking about the same order. But I will ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Karic said, "There's a telegram," what did he mean? Could you please assist Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- perhaps I didn't make my objection clear, and that's my fault. The objection is to -- to be clear, whether this witness saw whether Karic physically had the document or whether he's just in a position of having to draw conclusions and inferences. That's important because there's going to -- and I make it clear so that everyone understands. We've got some serious questions about this -- not questions against this witness but questions about this particular order and document, so we're very keen to make it clear whether the piece of paper was seen or not by Karic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we have to go slower, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, what did Karic say to you?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: No, Karic didn't say anything to me, but he told Sefer that there was a telegram from Delic that he had and he said authoritatively that the scaling-down of the operation was out of the question. I didn't see the document. I concluded that it refers to that document, but perhaps it does not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Karic said -- yeah, Karic says to Sefer that he has a telegram and then you said he said, "Authoritatively that the scaling-down" -- before Karic replied to his own answer -- to his own question, what was -- what was the question to Halilovic and what was his reply that you -- you heard?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: There was no question. It was Karic's assertion or remark in front of Sefer and he said to Sefer - he didn't ask him anything - "There is a letter for you from Delic," that they received up there in that place where they were, this group, Karic, Bilajac, Zicro. Sefer said, "I know. I received it." He didn't say anything more. Karic said, "A scaling-down of the operation is out of the question." Sefer said, "We're proceeding according to plan." There were no questions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ask Sefer what was the scale of the operation?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I did ask him once when the operation will begin. I don't know, he said that, the operation could make the position of President Izetbegovic easier for the negotiations, if it were to bear fruit, if it were to end successfully, something along those lines. On our way back - this is something else - from up there, then Cibo, he and I talked. Actually, Cibo said first that this was the biggest offensive since the beginning of the war, and Sefer said something along similar lines -- or Sefer said that about the offensive. I don't know exactly. But mostly Cibo and him and I spoke that if it was a success, then that would be the real thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So where did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. Perhaps I could just intervene again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to do this again. But I just noticed my learned friend has been putting to the witness the words "the operation." And I'd just like to point out that on the order that is there, which is the subject of this cross-examination, what's referred to is "plan --" I'm quoting now from the preamble: "Planned combat actions." And then in the first paragraph, there is a requirement -- an order to "re-examine the decision in the sense of a realistic estimate of forces and possibilities of carrying out of tasks." Now, I'm not suggesting that there was any attempt to mislead. We've all slipped into the use of the term from time to time. But it shouldn't proceed that the word "the operation" be used as arising out of this particular order, if indeed this is the order that's being referred to because the words "the operation" just aren't used in the paragraph that I've referred to, which seem to be the operative questions. And that has got some relevance to the case. I don't want to make a speech in front of the witness. You'll recall -- I won't say the name of it. But you'll recall the -- yes. I'll confine myself to saying Your Honours know why it is that I'm concerned about that matter. It's -- again, it's not a problem with the witness and frankly it's not a criticism of the Prosecutor there. It's -- it's just that I'm a bit touchy about the use of that term "the operation" in the context of the use of this order. So that's what I raise now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the best way is to use whatever is said in that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've actually moved on from the document. I'm just generally saying what was the conversation. And I think the witness did say - and I'll clarify it for him - from him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What word did he use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to me it's all right, but there might be some confusion which could be mixed up with other operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. May I clarify this from the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the document said "planned combat action."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, "combat action." And then later on he's talking about the conversations that Cibo and them are having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- about what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, and I take my learned friend's point that it's important to clarify this adds to what -- what they -- what they referred to it amongst themselves as they were conversing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, you heard the objection of my -- of learned Defence counsel. When they were talking about scaling down - and I'm not going to use the word - what word did they use? What was the word that they were using?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I can just read that it says: "To review the decision and bring it down to -- within realistic options." But that's all that I can say. Your Honours, in my book it's mentioned, because this happened later, but I didn't know at the time when the operation was underway that the operation was called "Neretva." In my -- when we were talking about it, or as it was going on, there was no reference to the Operation Neretva. Later, when I was speaking to Karic and so on, there was talk about what is that operation called of ours? I think Karic said "Mostar." I think Sefer also said "Mostar." I didn't think that they were trying to deceive me. But I really didn't know that it was called "Operation Neretva," even that there was a map that existed, which I saw for the first time in some newspaper that somebody published. Now I am using the term "operation," but at the time I never mentioned that in any report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hodzic, what was it that when they were discussing it -- and I'm not asking you to look at the order now, whatever the order says. Between themselves, what terminology did they use? When Karic says, you know, we've been asked to do this about whatever - I don't want to put any words in your mouth - what was the terminology between themselves, and Halilovic says, "I'm not going to do this"? What was the terminology between themselves that they were using?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: I have no clue. The military usually used the term "combat operation." Sometimes I would say "offensive." "Combat operations," [as interpreted] it was the most -- the most frequently used. But I cannot specifically say well, that's when Sefer said "operation" or -- or "offensive" or "combat activities" or that -- whoever said what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think, just to remind you again, Mr. Hodzic, we are still on the 12th of September. Then where did you go with Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I've just -- I apologise. I've interrupted numerous times now. This one is a translation issue that's been brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we just have a clarification for -- at page 104, line 7, the witness said: "Sometimes I would hear 'offensive.'" And then the next word has been rendered as "combat operations." Could we just is that the interpreter clarify that, because I'm instructed by the Bosnian speaker here that it was "combat activities" that was the word us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, the question was: Where did you go on the 12th with Sefer Halilovic? You were on your way somewhere.

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: We arrived at Dobro Polje, and on the way we were joined by the commander of the 45th Brigade from Neretvica, who had his unit up there, which was already close to these people from Prozor. And then we went to these fighters of Haso Hakalovic. Sefer was telling them something. We went through the forest. There were several groups there. Then we went to -- past the people from Prozor. Enver Buza was talking to them in the field about something, and Sefer very briefly. And I remember that he said at the time that, "Your task should be towards Vilica Guvno and to go towards," what's it called, Makljen, I think. And that's when an interesting thing happened, which I did not record, unfortunately. Mr. Halilovic addressed the group with Haso Hakalovic, and in several other places, and also the group from Prozor. He literally repeated everything to the fighters about how they should go -- like, he said in Kostajnica that they -- what I recorded and what you have, so that I don't have to repeat. I intended to record that, and because I always had a lot of problems and I didn't have enough film and I had even fewer cassettes, so I didn't want to waste the cassette. But I wished I could have taped that and I wish I had that, because I just thought, Well, as a journalist I don't need that any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that day, did Halilovic address the Prozor Independent Battalion once or twice?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Voljevac, and he addressed the fighters there, and that's the photo which you showed here, and he told them that the plan was to go to Crni Vrh for them, and then he again felt that he needed to address the fighters again from -- the fighters from Prozor and Neretvica, and we went back -- well, we had to go back anyway, to take that road back to Jablanica. There was no other road. And then when we got there, again he spoke to them. I didn't record it, but just based on my recollection. He briefly said that the offensive was starting tomorrow and that this just happened to coincide with the 13th of September, when he left the Yugoslav People's Army and joined -- came to Bosnia and Herzegovina and joined in the planning of the Patriotic League, and so on and so forth. And then one fighter said, "Long live the second Tito," and that's how it was. The mood was quite pleasant. The fighters were in a good mood. They were singing songs to Sefer Halilovic, to Alija Izetbegovic, to Buza, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the offensive start the next morning, on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of June [as interpreted], the offensive was supposed to begin from Bugojno to Mostar, throughout that whole area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hodzic. You said 13th of June. Do you mean 13th of September? The transcript reflects --

utterances.speaker: SEFKO HODZIC
utterances.text: September, yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] September, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe before we are going to the 13th of September we have to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay in The Hague for another day, and please remember that you are still under the oath during your stay in The Hague. So do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Madam Usher will show you out of the room, and I'll see you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have two minutes left for this sitting. Ms. Chana, could you please inform me how long --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are going to take to finish the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I was proceeding with all due speed. And I think the half an hour we lost this morning has impacted on my promise to finish in one session. But I would need exactly that, Your Honour, half an hour more, half an hour to 45 minutes, tops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. And, Mr. Morrissey? I'm not going to blame you on the 30 minutes we lost in the morning, but maybe you could brief me about how long you are going to take for the cross-examination so that we could decide whether we have to sit tomorrow afternoon or we could finish -- I mean, take a break before the Prosecution's -- after the Prosecution's case, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just considering really now, having heard the evidence, what the position is. There is the possibility of -- of a -- of a controlled cross-examination -- of a -- well, they should all be controlled, but a relatively short cross-examination. And I just need to reflect on that. Some -- the evidence has come out in a particular way. The witness hasn't really -- well, he's given his evidence live in a very detailed way. That certainly has had an impact on what I was going to ask him about a lot of things I was going to ask have come out. Would Your Honours permit me to -- to just think about this for a little while and communicate with the -- with Your Honours' associates this afternoon and, of course, with the Prosecution as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd like to make it short, if I can, and it's possible that that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He was going to be a long witness. Now, I think, possibly not so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course you could do that. And we have reserved tomorrow afternoon's sitting from 4.00 to 5.30. This is the -- the time that we could get. And I have to remind the parties that we'll have a 65 ter meeting in room 177 this afternoon at 2.30. And because of the space limit still, two people from each team is allowed to take part, at which we'll be talking about the future planning. That will not go into the substance of this case, so it's very off-record discussions. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned for this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
